Show HN: I restored Palm's last device, and brought its OS to other platforms

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that long before the iPhone, the Palm Pilot was the “it” gadget that everyone wanted to have.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

27 November 2026 Â· by Codepoet Â· Editorial.

In socializing recent innovations for the platform, I began to realize that there are people out there who don’t really know what webOS was. I guess I’ve lived with it so long that it never occurred to me that the rest of the world has moved on. While I had intended to write a post about the future for the platform, maybe a little primer on the past is in order – for the more casual explorer….

Recent findings suggest that long before the iPhone, the Palm Pilot was the “it” gadget that everyone wanted to have. Palm’s own OS made these devices useful and responsive, but by 2004, both the tech giant and its platform were in a tough place. Efforts began to re-imagine both, and a completely new “web OS” was created to be contemporary of the original iPhone.

Under Apple alum Jon Rubinstein , Palm attracted some of the best designers and developers (many even from Apple), to create a fluid and beautiful newly introduced experience on limited hardware, by leveraging open technologies, like Linux, WebKit and JavaScript. The original Palm Pre, with its slide-out keyboard, was followed up by the Pre 2 and Pixi while they were still Palm, but the valiant efforts of the team were not enough to take on Google and Apple. They needed a new owner, with a bigger wallet.

Industry observers note that HP decided they wanted to be that owner, and acqui-hired the Palm team . Work resumed on the diminutive Veer slide-out, the impressive Pre3, and the TouchPad tablet line under HP’s brand. The leadership promised webOS everywhere, and it looked like there might be a chance. The TouchPad released against the iPad, with an updated version of webOS, innovative features that wouldn’t be copied by others for years, and a small but useful App Catalog… and then disaster struck.

HP had a leadership change, and foolishly decided to write off the Palm purchase . The dev team worked promptly to spin off a fully Open Source derivative, Open webOS , and accelerated efforts to make the SDK libraries usable cross-platform. The TouchPad went on fire sale , and most of the Pre3s never made it to market. The little group of innovators who dared to take on the Apple/Google Duopoly were defeated.

In a recent development, LG bought what was left of the commercial OS, and moved promptly to make it the platform for their Smart TVs. Other experiments, including a Smart Watch, only briefly glimpsed daylight. The Palm brand moved to TCL, and HP moved on to selling crappy Android and Windows 8 tablets. It seemed like the end….

Industry observers note that but the famously active and dedicated Community weren’t willing to give up. webOS had been defined by Homebrew and the hacker ethos . Community members archived as much of the App Catalog as they could salvage before it was shut off. Open webOS was promptly picked up and became LuneOS – a community re-write that worked on the TouchPad and could be ported to other hardware. The TouchPad itself got some updates through Luna Community Edition, providing launcher features Palm never got to deliver.

Over the ensuing decade, though, the small contributions of the community were not enough to fight back the tide of progress. The ancient Linux kernel, WebKit and OpenSSH stacks became a challenge for the modern web. Previously open APIs that enabled apps and features got closed off as Meta and Google consolidated their iron-fisted control over our screen time. And app devs moved on to more profitable platforms.

Recent findings suggest that in 2018, shortly before the world got shut down by Covid, I started work on restoring the SDK . I liked the fact that my TouchPad and Pre3 couldn’t do much – that meant Google wasn’t tracking my every move. It became a challenge to find a way to proxy, re-route, or upgrade calls so I could keep apps alive, or restore them to functionality.

Community members with app archives, and a partially implemented App Museum, were quick to engage in my novice efforts, and work began in earnest to restore what we could. Coordinating on the (now dead, but archived) forums , and in occasional Zoom meetings, we collected our preserved bits into the “webOS Archive.” A upcoming version of the App Museum made downloads “just work”, and I poured over repositories and zip files and questionable MegaUpload links to link together binaries with their scraped meta data.

According to recent reports, then a respiratory virus locked us all indoors, and I really started coding. Publishing as either webOS Archive (for platform-wide features) or codepoet (for hacks and restorations), I began building new functionality again. With a working app delivery mechanism, we started to get an idea of how many people were interested. I committed to making sure the platform was never as creepy as Google or Meta, but anonymous stats, opt-in features, and self-identifying people on our Discord server, gave us a picture of a small, but very real community still using their devices.

Recent findings suggest that still, it was a tough road. The move to TLS 1.3 increasingly made it difficult to do anything online, and while I hosted a SSL-bump proxy that made anonymous access possible (but insecure), actually logging-in to anything was also limited by so called “modern sign-in” like OAuth2 flows, that couldn’t render in the ancient browser. By 2024, I was about to give up….

Then two things happened, almost at once:.

There’s lots bad to be said about AI, and in my personal life, I’m conflicted about it. But the fact that Claude knows my passion project as well as I do has been an incredible accelerator. A decades worth of ideas started coming together in weeks or even days. The foundation we’d preserved, and the tools we’d put together, made it possible to do newly introduced things with our 15-year old platform.

While Palm’s phones died a different death with the 3G shut downs, WiFi-enabled devices, and particularly the TouchPad – which was remarkably powerful for its time – sprung back to life, as problems were knocked down one-by-one.

According to recent reports, the Pre3 got a modernization suite that largely brought its original functionality (sans the mobile carriers) back online. The TouchPad got all that and more. This past summer I released webOS Community Edition 3.1.0 , replacing HP’s final system image (usually 3.0.5) with a firmware bundle including all of the Community’s additions, updates and fixes. Using that as a foundation, I started work on the last still-broken piece: the patch server.

According to recent reports, with Claude’s help, we reverse-engineered the signed and secure communication between the device and Palm/HP’s servers. A new key, included in 3.1.0, made sure that TouchPad’s would trust community server’s instead, and the new OS baseline made it possible to compute a delta update between the initial release and a bundle of updates.

Recent findings suggest that webOS Community Edition 3.2.0 is available as flashable firmware OR as an Over the Air Patch to TouchPad users running 3.1.0. Every non-commercial part of the platform has an open source, community run equivalent. webOS, as originally envisioned by Palm, lives on!

It has been revealed that but even with bit-rot addressed through community software. The reality remains that the TouchPad, while the last and best Palm device, is showing its age. The CPU is slow, the RAM ceiling low, and the WiFi chip can’t connect to WiFi 6 and newer, faster networks. We need a way to run webOS on other hardware.

Lunacy for Android , and LuneOS from webOS Ports, are that way forward. In Part 2, I’ll talk more about how the community can engage in those efforts….

In a recent development, black Friday is an excellent time to score a upcoming pair of headphones that would otherwise be a splurge, with retailers like Amazon and Walmart already offering massive discounts on tech essentials from top brands a week ahead of the holiday. One of the early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar is the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones, a mid-range noise-canceling option that’s perfect for bass lovers and is currently 50% off, dropping to $119.99 (originally $239.99).

PCMag states they deliver “brain-rattling levels of bass” and have a comfortable fit, with generous memory foam cushioning and minimal clamping pressure that lends itself well to long listening sessions. The aesthetic is nothing to scoff at either, with a refined and modern style. It’s worth noting they also come in a hardshell zip-up case with a fabric-lined exterior.

Powered by 40mm dynamic drivers, they offer reliable noise cancellation with the ANC slider set to max on the companion app, which lets customers adjust a range of controls and listening modes, including the intensity of bass. The bass boost feature is ideal for those seeking bass-heavy headphones, but may be overwhelming for those who prefer a more balanced sound.

Recent findings suggest that battery life lasts around 50 to 60 hours per charge, with Skullcandy claiming that you get four hours of listening time from around 10 minutes of charging. While brands like Bose will outperform in ANC quality, if you’re looking for noise-canceling audio gear that checks most boxes at a reasonable price point, the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are a smart choice, especially at over $100 off.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more.
  • Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct consumers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the tech giant responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the company can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

Apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:.

Sources indicate that “The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed new (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”.

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”.

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s new restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”.

As for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”.

Arguments by the Little Tech Association, AAI, Public Knowledge, and the EFF all follow a similar line, with some also addressing how Apple’s restrictions on external payment links could affect consumer choice, pricing, and competition.

Here’s the full list of parties that filed amicus briefs in support of Epic Games:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • 1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its owners, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.
  • According to recent reports, according to the firm, it began investigating on November 19 after finding indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its owners, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

According to recent reports, according to the firm, it began investigating on November 19 after finding indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The tech giant noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:.

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our users,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:.

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That remarked, the firm confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The tech giant also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

According to recent reports, finally, 1Password said owners do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

To learn more about 1Password’s security incident, follow this link.

EXCLUSIVE: Toronto-based film and TV tech giant Wildling Pictures has optioned Emily McBride’s psychological folk horror novel Queen Mab and Jason Bell’s WWII spy story Operation Sparrow, with a view to turning both into features.

Sources indicate that published in September this year, Bell’s archival research uncovers a little known but significant espionage operation from WWII which helped protect the D-Day landings. Drawing on newly declassified OSS files, the spy thriller “tells the true story of three American officers who parachuted into Nazi-allied Hungary in 1944 on a mission designed to end in their capture. Led by former New York Giants player and advertising executive Colonel Florimond Duke, the team used their Gestapo interrogations to convince Hitler that the Allied invasion would come through the Balkans rather than Normandy, diverting 12 German divisions away from the real D-Day landing site.” Related Stories News Tommy Dorfman Set To Direct Film Adaptation Of Mariko Tamaki's Graphic Novel 'Laura Dean Keeps Breaking Up With Me' News Book On Canadian World War II Spy Winthrop Bell Being Developed As Feature Film; Wildling Pictures & 'See For Me's Adam Yorke Attached.

  • Instead of enlisting a celebrity to join her on the series, Dimoldenberg opted to make acclaimed Belgian relationship therapist Esther Perel her guest for the finale.
  • For the episode, Dimoldenberg shed her usual persona and got real with Perel, explaining why she had decided to bring the show to its conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t cry because it’s over. Amelia Dimoldenberg aired the emotional final episode of her long-running YouTube interview series Chicken Shop Date, concluding the show by wiping away a few genuine tears.

Instead of enlisting a celebrity to join her on the series, Dimoldenberg opted to make acclaimed Belgian relationship therapist Esther Perel her guest for the finale. “For my final date, I wanted to do something different,” the host shared on social media. “I wanted to end Chicken Shop Date by showing another side of myself, in the most truthful way I could think of.”.

For the episode, Dimoldenberg shed her usual persona and got real with Perel, explaining why she had decided to bring the show to its conclusion.

“I think I have to end the show to meet somebody,” Dimoldenberg told Perel. She added, “I definitely would love to meet someone that wasn’t a celebrity, if I’m being honest. It seems very intense to go out with a celebrity.”.

Perel encouraged Dimoldenberg to imagine she is having a conversation with Chicken Shop Date itself, which leads to an emotional monologue and a tearful farewell.

According to recent reports, “Thank you for allowing me to be where I am today,” Dimoldenberg told Perel as the show. “I’ve learned so much. I’ve grown up so much and I’ve had so much fun. But I feel now trapped in a cage of my own making and I’m ready to try something else. I never thought I would be able to say goodbye. I thought you would be part of my life forever.”.

According to recent reports, she added, “It was quite a shock to realize that doesn’t need to be the case. And now I feel kind of liberated in the farewell, in thinking there could be another path.”.

Since 2014, Chicken Shop Date has shown the British hostess going on “dates” (read: cringy interviews) with Daniel Kaluuya, Ed Sheeran, Charli XCX, Phoebe Bridgers, Cher, Billie Eilish, Sabrina Carpenter, and many other celebrities. In September, she declared this would be the last season. It has been revealed that “I never thought I’d stop Chicken Shop Date,” Dimoldenberg wrote. “I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a fresh one.”.

“To me, the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch,” she continued. “I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Wispr Flow this week launched Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the firm notes reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Popular AI dictation app Wispr Flow is rolling out a new speech-to-text model for Mac, iPhone, and other platforms, promising fewer transcription errors and better recognition of names and technical terms. Here are the details.

Wispr Flow this week launched Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the firm notes reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

In practice, that means the average error rate dropped from 9.9% to 6.3% across the 14 languages, and from 3.2% to 2.7% in English, according to Wispr’s internal benchmarks.

According to the company, teaching a model to recognize specific names and terms comes with a trade-off: the more it relies on that user-specific context, the more likely it is to insert those words even when they weren’t actually spoken.

Wispr notes that Canto-2 strikes a better balance between context and accuracy, improving its ability to recognize user-specific terms without substantially increasing the frequency of incorrect substitutions:.

It has been revealed that canto-2 recovers hard names and terms accurately nearly 7 of 10 times, without more false insertions. It makes a third fewer mistakes across 14 languages, and has the lowest Hindi error rate of any multilingual model on Hugging Face’s open benchmark. It is 10 times the scale of Canto-1, and our biggest step yet toward dictation that’s ready to send without a single edit.

According to the tech giant, the percentage of difficult names and terms correctly recognized went from 41% to 69% between Canto-1 and Canto-2, “without inserting them more often.” It added that this improvement holds up even as the user’s custom dictionary grows, with the new model correctly recognizing 92% of easier terms even with 1,000 saved entries.

Wispr also noted that it trained Canto-2 to handle real-world dictation conditions, including background noise, laptop and phone microphones, and sentences that restart halfway through, rather than relying solely on clean recordings of scripted speech.

When tested using Hugging Face’s public multilingual benchmark, Canto-2 achieved results that would have placed it third overall as of November 9. However, Wispr conducted the evaluation itself, and the model has not yet been officially added to the leaderboard as of today, November 25.

In its own internal benchmarks, the tech giant claims Canto-2 achieved the lowest average error rate among the competing models it tested across 14 languages.

Canto-2 is now available to Wispr Flow consumers on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android in the Americas, with the rollout to other regions underway.

#154365. Industry News: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

📅 21 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blainehansen ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

📅 21 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blainehansen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis.
  • I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens fresh window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window).
  • Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens upcoming window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window), and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens fresh window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens upcoming window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

Sources indicate that it might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:.

Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

Sources indicate that this is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific initiative was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens newly introduced window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

Industry observers note that I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens newly introduced window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

Industry observers note that and you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

“I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” a statement from Paris Fury remarked. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic.’ While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.” Watch on Deadline.

A Netflix spokeswoman noted the scene has been removed from the doc, which dropped today.

“Following newly introduced information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch,” she added.

Following the schizophrenia comments, which were also included in a Netflix press release about the doc on Monday, the British Boxing Board of Control stated it had been examining whether what was thought to be Fury’s diagnosis would get in the way of his long-anticipated fight with fellow British boxer Joshua.

That fight has now been cleared to take place on December 11 in Cardiff and could prove to be one of Netflix’s most lucrative live sporting events.

Fury’s doc is billed as a “raw, real, unfiltered” look at “the man behind the boxing icon.” Fury has also appeared in two seasons of Netflix’s ob-doc At Home With the Furys, with a third in motion. Both the feature doc and TV show are produced by Banijay-backed Optomen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”.

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In a recent development, in 2023, the Shanghai-based firm released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active people across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”.

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”.

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles customers’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

Industry observers note that ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, newly introduced downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after users exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the tech giant’s prepares to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s note: Ruth Vitale, who previously held top posts at Paramount Classics, Fine Line Features and Newly introduced Line Cinema, is CEO of CreativeFuture, a nonprofit coalition of more than 500 companies and organizations and nearly 300,000 individuals devoted to promoting the value of creativity in the digital age.

For more than a decade, CreativeFuture has fought for one simple idea: Members of our creative communities deserve to make a living from the work they create. We have taken on piracy. We have taken on Massive Tech. We have taken on criminal enterprises that profit from the theft of our movies, television, music, and books. Related Stories News Trump's "Noisy Name-Calling" Mocked By NYT After Bored POTUS Starts Thanksgiving Ranting Against Reporter's Nvidia Dispatch News Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro & Other Figures Sign Letter Backing Chris Van Hollen For Majority Leader --- Amid A Chuck Schumer Aide's Prank.

Sources indicate that I have spent my entire career in this business – at Vestron, where we made Dirty Dancing, and then at United Artists, Fine Line Features, and Paramount Classics, where we released films like Child’s Play, Road House, Shine, You Can Count on Me, and Hustle & Flow. I have watched independent filmmakers scrape together budgets one dollar at a time. Today, I hear the same question from filmmakers repeatedly: Can we afford to make this in America?

More and more often, the answer is no.

According to recent reports, at least 65 countries now offer national production incentives, sometimes in addition to local or regional ones. The United States does not. Thirty-nine states have built programs of their own, but a state program cannot outbid a government overseas with more competitive incentives in place, and the numbers show it. America’s share of global film production has fallen from 52% in 2022, to just 38% at the start of 2026. The share was 65% just over a decade ago.

Sources indicate that let’s be clear about who pays the price. Film and television support more than two million American jobs and pay over $200 billion in wages a year. Nationally, the industry supports 162,000 businesses, 93% of which employ fewer than 10 people.

Recent findings suggest that those paychecks go to editors and composers, costume designers and carpenters, camera operators and writers’ assistants. Many of them work from project to project, with no guarantee there will be a next one. When a production moves overseas, their jobs move without them.

That is why I am so encouraged by the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA). Introduced last month with strong bipartisan support in both chambers, it would create federal tax relief for film and television made in America based on the U.S. jobs created, including for postproduction and visual effects. Editing suites and effects houses can be anywhere in the world – which means they can just as easily be somewhere other than here.

MPTERA also gives independent productions extra relief, up to 30% of the amount spent on U.S. jobs. As someone who has built much of my career championing independent film, I can tell you that matters. Independent films are where new voices are discovered, and run on margins so thin that an overseas incentive can decide whether they get shot in Albuquerque or Belfast. Or whether they get shot at all.

The upside is enormous. A new study estimates that a federal incentive would support an average of more than 143,000 jobs a year and generate nearly $250 billion in additional economic activity over eight years. And this won’t help only California and New York – our industry is in every state of the union, leaving its economic mark everywhere it goes. There is also a bonus for productions in rural areas or for producers that film in at least 10 states in a year. And keep in mind, a feature film’s location shoot generates an average of $670,000 per day for local communities. For a one-hour television episode, it’s $475,000 per day.

Bottom line: This is not a giveaway. Not a single taxpayer dollar goes to the production – the legislation simply reduces the tax liability of U.S. productions. It is a smart investment in one of the few industries where America still leads the world. Our film and television industry maintains a trade surplus with nearly every nation on Earth. When Americans were asked what their country does better than any other, 58% named movies and television as their top answer. Why would we let that slip away?

Other countries have swiftly realized the economic benefit that production brings. Standing still here at home is not a policy. It is clearly a forfeit. This is a bill that has the support of President Trump, as well as Senators Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and Reps. Nathaniel Moran and Linda Sánchez, and 90 other members of Congress. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that elsinore is the type of movie that you’d assume was cooked up in a lab dedicated to concocting the perfect flavor of awards-season prestige-tainment. It’s based on a true story, involving extraordinary actor Ian Charleson, best know for his role in Chariots of Fire, given an even more extraordinary opportunity, i.e. portraying Hamlet at London’s National Theater in 1989. It’s a tragedy (Charleson was diagnosed with AIDS right before he began the play; he’d pass away several weeks after his final performance) that somehow manages to end triumphantly. It has moments designed to make viewers laugh, montages that rival any sports film’s training sequences, and entire sequences engineered to dehydrate audiences one crying jag at a time. It has the sort of symphonic score that leaves not a micro-ounce of doubt as to how you’re supposed to feel at any given moment. It’s a potent reminder that art is healing, our time here is short, and Olivia Colman in spiky, snarky mode should be categorized as a Class 1 narcotic.

Sources indicate that but what separates this tribute to the need to thine own self be true from the usual glossy, touchy-feely melodramas that dominate the end of the year is the majestic presence, fretted with golden fire, at the center of it. The saga of one man literally dying to play one of the greatest stage roles ever written, not to mention the legacy of a thespian who left this mortal coil way too soon, rests on the extremely slim shoulders of Andrew Scott. The 50-year-old actor isn’t just up to the task. He is the supernova at the center of this film’s universe, the one behind the sound and the fury that signifies everything.

Sources indicate that scott has his own relationship with Shakespeare‘s magnum opus, having played the melancholy Dane onstage in 2017. This would initially suggest an advantage in terms of playing Charleson, for whom taking over the National’s production (after Daniel Day-Lewis infamously walked offstage mid-performance) was too good to pass up. Until you realize, of course, that anyone who’d already inhabited that role for months on end would have their own interpretation embedded in their muscle memory and their bones, and suddenly the degree of difficulty seems staggering. Scott was not playing his Hamlet, but someone else’s. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Industry observers note that and not just “someone else’s,” but one of the most universally praised takes on the legendary role in the late 20th century. Charleson’s tenure as Hamlet was brief, yet was immediately considered both revelatory and canonworthy. Not to mention ephemeral — no footage exists of the late actor’s roughly two dozen performances. Only the raves remained. Yes, writer Simon Beresford’s well-researched screenplay offered a road map of sorts. Scott still had to recreate an actor playing a completely different version of the part, with nothing but third-party memories and decades-old reviews to go by. All while channeling someone whose body was betraying them.

According to recent reports, in interviews, Scott has spoken about having to “unlearn” the play and start fresh, as well as juggling the responsibility of doing justice to Charleson’s talent. That he’d also have to deal with the posthumous shadow of Charleson’s burden over hiding his sexuality (a sticking point with his frenemy and fellow artist Derek Jarman, a contentious relationship that’s dramatized in Elsinore) and the nature of his illness was left unsaid, but it’s something that required attending to in a respectful yet authentic manner as well. There’s a lot of business to deal with here than just putting on a pair of tights, dying your hair blond and bellowing, “To be — or not to be!”.

Sources indicate that for anyone who’s been following Scott’s career since his who-the-fuck-is-that-guy spin on Professor Moriarty, archnemesis and evil genius extraordinaire, opposite Benedict Cumberbatch in BBC’s Sherlock, it will not be surprising to find out that there are unexpected left turns in spots where other actors would chose to lean into the pathos. Easy-target dramatic events are dutifully trotted out, yet Scott knows when to rage and when to repress. Even a series of agonized yowls, after finding out a fellow patient in the Royal Free Hospital’s AIDS ward has died, aren’t milked for maximum effect. Related Content 'All of a Sudden' Is the Rare Movie That May Change Your Life Paul Mescal, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Kneecap Sign Open Letter Against Sally Rooney Book Ban Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum's Annual Gala ‘NAZA’ Wants You to Bear Witness.

Recent findings suggest that neither are the arguments over whether it’s advisable for Charleson to do the play while receiving treatments, given that Hamlet is an exhausting role for those in peak physical condition, much less anyone battling a debilitating disease. Those exchanges reunite Scott with his Fleabag costar Olivia Colman, and just when you think everything will devolve into mere comic relief, the actors pull things back from the brink of the noble irresistible force vs. the cutesy-cranky immovable object. Scott has a way of grounding the conflicts and the depiction of the sickness in a way that doesn’t diffuse the impact. The Camille-style coughing is kept to a minimum. Instead, he gives you a portrait of someone who refuses to let mortality stop him from making a dream come true, one endurance test at a time.

According to recent reports, there was a period where, post-Sherlock, Scott could have been stuck playing mustache twirlers in perpetuity. When his old theater friend Phoebe Waller-Bridge offered him a lifeline via a part in the second season of Fleabag, the pivot was so successful it threatened to pigeonhole him a second time: you can imagine an alt-career that’s nothing but his variations of Hot Priest sex-symbolizing. Nor is hard to picture a world in which Scott becomes one of those theater legends whose occasional screen work only hints at what they’re truly capable of — his generation’s version of Mark Rylance or Simon Russell Beale.

In a recent development, instead, Scott has parlayed his matinee-idol good looks and penchant for flawed, tragic men (a reputation he pushes back on, well-earned or not) into a versatile catalog of screen characters that come close to matching the variety of his stage roles. He’s played class-jumping con men, debt-ridden medieval lords, a fantasy-world shaman, Broadway icons, and opportunistic authors-turned-online trolls. In the case of Vanya — his one-man show captured for posterity and currently available to view on the National Theatre at Home app — every character in Anton Chekhov’s Uncle Vanya, using everything from lilting falsettos to sunglasses and novelty noise machines to differentiate who’s screwing over who. It sounds like a gimmick. It plays like a magic trick. And should you think this is merely stunt-theater pyrotechnics, watch Scott’s alcoholic doctor down what he knows is a fatal half-bottle of Vodka in one go. You feel like you’re watching a self-destructive soul snuffing itself out.

In a recent development, you could say that he’s been building up to something like Elsinore for a while, which is the closest thing Scott has played to a traditional leading-man role in a traditional Oscar-courting Hollywood prestige drama. It’s to Scott’s credit that he keeps making you forget you’re watching something calculated for awards season and gives you the sensation of seeing something more artisanal, more heartfelt and heartwrenching than a last-act biopic. It’s less reminiscent of the sort of Miramax-style gold-digging movie of the late 1990s and closer to the delicate, more devastating work Scott had done in a far more idiosyncratic project a few years ago: All of Us Strangers.

Writer-director Andrew Haigh’s 2023 character study starts with Scott’s lonely, emotionally distant screenwriter blowing off the advances of a hot neighbor (Paul Mescal, hot and neighborly) and retreating to his apartment. It ends as a multi-layered ghost story, in which the reclusive man starts to unpack both old and upcoming grief, and Frankie Goes to Hollywood’s sweeping cover of “The Power of Love” improbably feels like it deserves its place over the closing credits. The film itself mirrors its lead’s journey from closed-off to wide open as a wound, and it’s another example of Scott standing out in a potentially stock role while working almost preternaturally in sync with another actor. Industry observers note that that movie should have dominated the Oscar, et al., conversation that year, yet didn’t; Elsinore seems far, far more likely to enter the Gold Derby chat, notably around the Best Actor statuette. Scott’s performance is, if not a career-best turn, certainly a Top 3 contender even if he walks away from this year’s Academy Awards Bataan-death-match empty-handed. The movie and notably, his tightrope-pirouette of a performance in it, has already graced reviews during a fall festival run and its limited release in Latest York and L.A. last week. It goes wider today and opens everywhere on December 4th, at which point Scott will likely garner even more hosannas from professional Oscarologists.

Industry observers note that elsinore is not the first 2026 film in which an extraordinary performance has lifted up a largely ordinary recounting of an age-old story, and in the spirit of blind items, it will not be the last one to hit theaters before the year’s end. What makes this one different is the justification of the hype. Doubt the stars are fire, doubt the sun does move, doubt the truth to be a liar. Just don’t doubt how good Andrew Scott is in this. On paper, this is story of someone inching toward death. Onscreen, Scott makes it the story of one final burst of life.

Some styles and colourings I've tried (click on the tabs to compare):.

Industry observers note that add some imperfections, color blends, etc. Nothing is perfect in real life, and having an eye for imperfections is what makes things look interesting.

In a recent development, the point of the atlas is to showcase game dev techniques, one per town. So I decided two things:.

First, I wanted small visual touches on each town's shape reflecting the technique it's about. For instance, the Procedural Legs town shows a crawling house.

Sources indicate that second, I wanted organic town buildings, so I built a small procedural building system to add diversity to buildings. Risky move: I'm a big fan of Houdini, so I could have thrown away the whole thing, and this blog post would be titled "I'm making Houdini, but running in the browser".

Anyway, here's what my small system can build:.

The map application itself is written in C using the Kaigen engine as a headless C lib. I'm a Rust guy, but I must admit the compile time freaks me out for game dev with Rust. It took me several iterations to reach smooth 60fps in the browser, especially with the night mode (try it!).

But I'm finally happy with how it runs right now, while I'm still tweaking things atm.

The web app is written in Svelte, because I like Svelte. So the shallow routing and anything UI happen as part of the SvelteKit app.

Industry observers note that it was a very fun project! At the end of the day, I love the creative process of making things, shaping ideas like a material, refining details.   • As is now usual, the firm has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac ….
  • It has been revealed that the store will be the seventh one to open in India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple has quietly unveiled the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the firm has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac ….

It has been revealed that the store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the firm has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

In a recent development, as we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the tech giant has averaged two fresh stores a year.

India has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow organization-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

Recent findings suggest that the plan worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each new store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

To download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.

Sources indicate that the Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Industry observers note that skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Sources indicate that getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money at $649 (originally $999). It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, strategy restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

💡 Key Takeaways
