  • Recent findings suggest that while Amazon excels in convenience and variety, that same abundance can be overwhelming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

According to recent reports, we have Amazon to thank (or blame) for completely transforming the way we shop. The e-commerce giant’s virtually endless product selection, massive inventory, and ultra-fast delivery options have made everything from streaming movies to ordering groceries from Whole Foods as easy as clicking a button.

Recent findings suggest that while Amazon excels in convenience and variety, that same abundance can be overwhelming. Sifting through dozens of near-identical products can lead to decision fatigue, leaving many consumers frustrated or simply burned out. That’s just one reason more customers are exploring alternatives to Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that some want to support smaller businesses and independent creators instead of contributing to the fortune of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, whose net worth reportedly exceeds $270 billion. Others have grown uneasy about the manufacturer’s business practices and environmental impact, prompting them to take their spending elsewhere.

According to recent reports, although Amazon has made efforts to promote small businesses on its platform, its market dominance still makes some shoppers hesitant. If you’re among those looking to support independent sellers and ethical brands, there are plenty of great options available.

According to recent reports, sites like Etsy let you buy directly from makers and designers, while platforms such as Uncommon Goods showcase work from independent artists on everything from gifts to home decor. Shopping for bigger-ticket items? There are several excellent Amazon alternatives that offer great deals, some even matching or beating Amazon.

Right now, we’re in the middle of Black Friday and Cyber Monday, two of the biggest shopping holidays of the year. While Amazon is offering plenty of exclusive deals on its website, shoppers looking for other places to browse will find a growing list of online retailers offering more curated, mindful, or ethical shopping experiences.

Industry observers note that many of these sites streamline your search by carefully selecting products, saving you from endless scrolling. Plus, eco-conscious and socially responsible shoppers will appreciate that several of these companies are certified B Corporations, meaning they meet rigorous standards for transparency, sustainability, and ethical business practices.

Keep reading for some of the best non-Amazon places to shop online, whether you’re hunting for handmade gifts, stylish essentials, or deals that don’t require a Prime membership.

And if you’re perusing any of these sites for holiday gifts, keep in mind that shipping deadlines are approaching faster than you might think. Hanukkah begins in just a few days, so you’ll want to start ordering now. Christmas Eve falls on Dec. 24, with many retailers’ holiday shipping cutoffs landing around Dec. 15.

Best for travel, outdoors, and sports apparel and accessories.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for clothing, footwear, outdoor gear, and sports equipment, the best Amazon alternative is REI. Founded as a consumer cooperative, REI has long been able to use its membership dues to fund projects that promote conservation, diversity, and equity. To this day, $5 from the purchase of every lifetime membership is donated to the REI Cooperative Action Fund, which supports organizations “working to improve the health and well-being of people and communities through time spent outside.”Of course, you don’t have to be a member anymore to shop the best REI deals online (though members do get additional perks and discounts). We’ve been shopping at REI for years to get hard-to-find products or trip-specific gear, and the site continues to grow with unique product offerings and newly introduced brands today. Right now, they’re offering up to 50% off on all clearance products. Start your search at REI.com.

Best for groceries, supplements, and snacks.

In a recent development, certified B Corporation Thrive Market rolled out in 2014 with a cause-driven mission to offer organic and natural groceries and other sustainable products at affordable prices. The membership-based online grocer allows shoppers to save 25 to 50 percent on more than 6,000 products spanning healthy foods, meat, pantry staples, wine, bath and body products, beauty and skincare, baby care, supplements, and home goods.Membership plans start at $5 per month (based on an annual subscription price of $59.95), and you can shop by diet and lifestyle (vegan, vegetarian, non-GMO, keto, paleo, raw, and more) as well as by values such as non-toxic, Environmental Working Group-verified, certified organic, cruelty-free, and others. We love using Thrive Market to stock up on groceries and pantry items, household goods, and everyday essentials, and their meat and seafood selection is surprisingly fresh. We’ve also found some of our favorite snacks and (sort of) good-for-you sweets through their marketplace, which stocks unique items from around the world. The site also has hard-to-find organic and specialty brands, which you can’t get at the big-box chains or on Amazon. Start shopping at ThriveMarket.com. Thrive Market offers promo codes, discounts, and deals all the time, too. See the latest offers here.

Best for fast, same-day delivery on everything from restaurants to retail.

According to recent reports, amazon may be known for Prime and its promise of two-day shipping (or sometimes even faster), but when you need something today, DashPass, DoorDash’s membership program, is the service we always turn to. Starting at just $9.99 per month — with a discounted $4.99 student strategy — DashPass unlocks $0 delivery fees on everything DoorDash has to offer, including restaurants, grocery stores, retail shops, florists, and local fan favorites.

Sources indicate that we’ve been loyal DashPass members for the past five years, and we genuinely wouldn’t switch to another delivery platform. It’s saved us more times than we can count, whether packing for a last-minute vacation, scrambling to send a gift, stocking up on simple things like paper towels (mid-cleaning session), or simply ordering a Gatorade after a night out when walking across the street somehow felt like too much.

In a recent development, yes, you can buy men’s clothing on Amazon, but instead of turning to off-brand names that will fall apart the first time you wash them, we suggest turning to a retailer we’ve known and trusted for decades: Men’s Wearhouse. The men’s shopping platform has everything you’ll need to stock up this fall and change out your seasonal wardrobe, from sweaters to suit sets and even scarves.

Best for pantry items and household goods.

Industry observers note that think of HiveBrands.com as your favorite general store or emporium, filled with unique snacks, drinks, health and beauty products, and household goods. Almost all of the options are sustainably made, ethically sourced, and from socially conscious companies. But they’re also just great products too — think organic nut butter and homemade sauces for the pantry, and clean soaps and lotions for your skincare routine. We’ve found super gentle and eco-friendly cleaning supplies and bug sprays, too.Everything ships in recyclable boxes printed with non-toxic ink and filled with 100% recyclable packing materials. Every order is carbon-neutral, too. What we like: Hive lets you shop by cause, whether you want to support brands helping small communities improve their livelihood, brands dedicated to championing equality, or female-owned businesses. You can shop by your preferred attributes too — like cruelty-free, Made in the USA, vegan-friendly, and more.

In a recent development, sure, you can order fresh flowers with your Amazon Prime account for delivery, but we prefer to go through a site like 1-800-Flowers instead. The online retailer has been around since the eighties and is our go-to for everything from beautiful rose bouquets to gift baskets and table arrangements that can be sent directly to you.

The site even lets you shop by occasion, making it simple to browse everything from sympathy arrangements to celebratory bunches. Depending on where you live in the United States, 1-800-Flowers offers same-day delivery (which often beats even Amazon’s fastest shipping option). You never have to worry about missing a birthday, graduation, or housewarming again — well, at least when it comes to flowers. You’ll still have to remember to RSVP.

Best for paperbacks, ebooks, and gifts.

According to recent reports, readers flock to Amazon every day to snag the latest novel they’ve been eyeing or the book everyone seems to be talking about after it was turned into a feature film. But here’s a trick: You don’t have to turn to the massive conglomerate to get the newest titles. You can find just as good — if not better — editions through Bookshop.

In a recent development, when you shop this way, you’re not sending more money to a billionaire who already has more than $270 billion. Instead, you’re supporting independent bookstores, because with each purchase, 30% of the sale goes to a smaller seller of your choice, according to the site.

Best for health/personal care products and cleaning supplies.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a one-stop eco-conscious shop for non-toxic and cruelty-free household supplies, beauty and skincare, personal care, and wellness products, and also want to save yourself from the hassle of last-minute restocks, then you’ll want to try Grove. The online subscription service offers everything from dishwasher and bathroom soap refills to medicine cabinet essentials and compostable plastic bags (and much more) from popular brands such as Dr. Bronner’s, Seventh Generation, Method, Mrs. Meyer’s Clean Day, Tom’s of Maine, and others, alongside independent names.It works like this: You’ll add product subscriptions that you can customize by frequency — say, you need dish soap and sponges every month and laundry detergent every three months. So long as your order meets the minimum of $29, you’ll get all of your must-haves in regular deliveries, efficiently packed in recyclable materials. Oh, and it’s a B Corp., too. Start shopping at Grove.co.

Best for sending gift baskets, special treats, and flowers.

Harry & David is our top pick for special occasions, offering a wide selection of gift baskets, flowers, wine, and sweet treats. The brand ships nationwide, and they also provide expedited shipping if you’re on a tight schedule or working with a deadline.

Best for original online jewelry gifts and buying conflict-free diamonds.

If you’re in the market for a jewelry gift, one place we recommend looking is Blue Nile. Founded in 1999, the brand is the original online jewelry retailer and still one of the most trusted sources for diamond jewelry. The retailer sources conflict-free diamonds and offers education services for choosing the right pieces. They’ve since expanded to other types of jewelry, but diamonds remain their bread and butter. Plus, Blue Nile has impeccable customer service, ensuring that the ordering and any follow-up processes are painless.

In a recent development, we’re not alone in our appreciation for Blue Nile. Helen Mirren, Brooklyn Decker, Grimm star Bitsie Tulloch, and Giuliana Rancic are just a few celebrities who have been spotted wearing Blue Nile jewelry on red carpets.

Best for designer apparel and everyday essentials.

From designer apparel to everyday essentials, Nordstrom’s markdowns give shoppers the chance to invest in pieces that last, often with free shipping and easy returns, making the experience stress-free.

What makes Nordstrom’s website even more tempting is the selection of brands on sale. You can score deals on favorites like On Running, Nike, Rag & Bone, plus home essentials from Voluspa candles and Calvin Klein bed sheets. Whether you’re updating your sneaker rotation, refreshing your wardrobe, or stocking up on skincare, Nordstrom’s curated deals make it easy to shop for quality brands.

Best for workout (and athleisure) apparel, accessories, and footwear.

Industry observers note that training for a marathon? Heading to a upcoming workout class? Lululemon has an incredibly versatile selection of everything from top-tier running shorts made for performance to bright tanks and tees that will have you standing out in a sea of neutrals. Over the last few years, Lululemon has worked to expand beyond the yoga studio (especially in the men’s department) with high-performance workout gear and ultra-comfy everyday clothing, and their styles frequently go viral for a reason. Instead of picking up cheap bike shorts that’ll ride up or pill immediately, this is a great place to shop for quality fitness gear that will last you through every workout (and every season).

Best for clothing, accessories, fitness equipment, and hiking equipment.

One of our favorite Amazon alternatives to shop these days is Huckberry.com. Once best known as an outdoor site, Huckberry’s online inventory now includes footwear, clothing, grooming, workout equipment, and even home decor. The site is pioneering what they call the “Everyday Adventure” category, which “sits between the traditional outdoor and fashion industries” while combining “the best of retail, media, and community.” The best part is that Huckberry offers a number of brands that you can’t find on Amazon, including newly introduced and emerging American designers. Their prices (and deals) are often pretty competitive too.

Best for a long-term subscription.

Sources indicate that sure, you can order ground or whole coffee beans on Amazon, but what you should really be turning to is Trade Coffee. Trade is a subscription-based service designed to cater to your individual tastes, helping match you with coffee that fits your preferences. It’s affordable, customized, and supports smaller businesses, so you can feel good about what’s in your cup with every sip.

Best for home goods, skincare, and bath and beauty.

One of the biggest perks of ordering through Amazon Prime is the lightning-fast shipping — you can get whatever you need, from clothing to sleep aids like melatonin to last-minute accessories before an upcoming event or concert, delivered in less than two days.

So if you’re in that same kind of rush and need something ASAP, we turn to Revolve. The online retailer offers the latest in fashion, popular viral products, beauty, and accessories, with shipping speeds that rival Prime. They offer several delivery options, including next day by 12 PM, next day by 8 PM, and 2nd Day Air, in addition to standard free shipping within 3–5 business days.

In our experience, they’ve never let us down when we’ve needed something in a pinch. Between the impressive product selection and expedited delivery options, Revolve is our go-to when we need an order fast.

Best for fashion, home essentials, and toys.

Macy’s has long been a favorite of ours for just about… anything. The major retailer, which was first established in 1858, offers an extensive lineup of fashion, beauty, personal care products, home goods, décor, and more. What we like most is the fast shipping; many items can be delivered in just a few days, along with consistent sales and exclusive perks through its VIP membership program.

One standout feature we especially love: In 2021, Macy’s partnered with WHP Global to bring back Toys “R” Us, the nostalgic, once-beloved toy retailer, both online and in select brick-and-mortar locations. On Macy’s site, you can find all the classic offerings, from Barbie and LEGO sets to games and puzzles, in a dedicated section that keeps the brand’s iconic rainbow aesthetic alive. There are even some toys created exclusively for Macy’s, per the brand’s site.

According to recent reports, it captures the same fun, variety, and affordable pricing that made Toys “R” Us so popular in the early 2000s. Only now, you can add it all to your cart from the comfort of home.

Best for home decor and gift items.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking to add globally-inspired flavors or flair to your cooking or home decor, World Market (or Cost Plus World Market) is our go-to for fair-trade products that meet sustainability and ethical standards. The San Francisco-founded retailer stocks gourmet groceries, fair-trade coffee and teas, international pantry essentials, handwoven baskets, kitchen accessories, vintage-inspired home furnishings, and more from every corner of the world.We’ve picked up everything from lamps and pillows to chocolates and flowers from the store, which has an eclectic array of offerings. It’s a great place to shop for unique gifts, too, if you want an Amazon alternative.Can’t wait for your delivery, but need the convenience of online shopping? You can opt for same-day Curbside Pickup at your local store and score an additional 15% off when you join the tech giant’s free membership program. Start shopping at WorldMarket.com.

Best for pet food, toys, and accessories.

In a recent development, what began as founder Dave Bolotsky’s virtual handmade marketplace has grown into one of the best places for shopping for handmade and one-of-a-kind gifts. Go to Uncommon Goods if you’re looking for cool finds by independent brands, designers, and makers. They’ve got everything from stylish jewelry and clothing to gourmet condiments and kitchen accessories to puzzles and home decor. This is our go-to site for unique gifts for birthdays, holidays, weddings, graduations, and more. We’ve purchased a lot of personalized gifts from Uncommon Goods, from wall art to toys to desk accessories.Vegans will be happy to know that the ethical online retailer only stocks leather-, feather-, and fur-free products. Many of their products are made from recyclable materials and packaging.The B corporation also donates $1 from every purchase to a nonprofit partner, uses eco-friendly packaging, pays its employees more than double the federal minimum wage, and advocates for paid family leave and better pay in the state of New York. Now, what’s a better Amazon alternative than that? Start shopping at UncommonGoods.com.

Best for getting freshly baked goods delivered to your door.

Industry observers note that amazon Fresh offers a wide selection of baked goods, from breads and pastries to other doughy favorites — but there’s another firm giving it serious competition: Wildgrain. Founded in 2020, Wildgrain is a subscription-based service that, according to the brand, “delivers artisan breads, pastas, and pastries straight to your door”. The process is simple: You choose when your box arrives, what’s inside — including vegetarian or gluten-free options — and your preferred price range. Boxes start at just $69 and cap at around $189.

With hundreds of five-star reviews, Wildgrain is praised for its convenience and simplicity. Every item is made with good-for-you ingredients, giving you that fresh-from-the-bakery taste without ever leaving home. Get started here.

Best for crafts, decor, gift ideas, and DIY designs.

From fan-made merch to home decor and accessories, Etsy features thousands of sellers offering unique, often handmade goods for purchase. Once known as a destination for DIY crafters, Etsy is now a full-service marketplace that sells everything from vintage clothing and antiques to jewelry, tableware, and furniture. Etsy is one of our go-to destinations for gifting, with one-of-a-kind picks for Halloween, housewarmings, and the holidays alike. Unlike Amazon, there’s no Etsy warehouse — only a network of artisans and local sellers who sell and ship their goods directly to you. Start shopping here.

According to recent reports, no list of the best alternatives to Amazon would be complete without mentioning Walmart. This mega discount superstore could be considered the original Amazon, as it offers daily competitive deals on a wide range of goods, from pantry products to clothing items and even pharmacy delivery. Walmart truly has everything you could possibly need, all in one place.

Best overall Amazon alternative.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to beat the Big Red Bullseye’s ridiculously convenient shopping options, especially on days like Prime Day, where Target often offers the same, if not lower, prices than Amazon. Target makes it easy to place an online order for deodorant, groceries, and bath towels and pick up your goods in-store or via its Drive Up option (simply wait in your car, and store staff will bring your purchases to you), or get everything delivered using Shipt’s same-day service.On top of its vast inventory, the mass retailer also offers a 5% discount whenever you use its RedCard debit or credit card. Don’t forget the retail giant’s smartphone app, which also boasts additional Target Circle deals. Is it as niche or as small a business to support like some of the other sites on our list? No. But does it deliver a ton of deals and exclusives that make it a worthy Amazon competitor? One hundred percent. Start shopping at Target.com.

How you feel about Amazon may also be the same way you feel about Temu, the Chinese e-tailer that offers millions of discount items for home and travel. Where else can you get $3 headphones or a $30 pizza oven? Like Amazon, Temu has millions of items in stock, from electronics to clothing to household essentials. Most of their items are made in China and are noticeably cheaper than those on Amazon, though shipping may take a few extra days if the products are coming from overseas. In our experience, you also get what you pay for. But if you need something in bulk or just want to test out a trend or viral product before committing to the real thing, Temu could be a good option for you.Of course, you’ll want to read up on Temu’s business practices before you decide whether or not you want to spend your money there. Congressional lawmakers have cited Temu’s sale of knockoff designer items and have asked the manufacturer for increased safety and compliance controls. A potential bright spot? Temu talks up its tree planting program, which partners with Trees for the Future to plant trees across Africa to benefit farmers in this region. Learn more here.

Industry observers note that tim Chan is the VP of Commerce at Penske Media, overseeing fashion, tech, lifestyle, and streaming coverage across marquee brands like Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, Variety, and WWD, among others. Previously, Chan was the first-ever Lifestyle Editor at Rolling Stone, covering all things fashion, culture, and travel through an entertainment lens. In addition to PMC, his bylines over the years have appeared in L’Uomo Vogue, Vogue Italia, Vogue Korea, i-D, and more. Chan has also consulted for a number of fashion brands, advising them on media and marketing strategy. He graduated from Columbia University with a master’s degree in journalism.

Recent findings suggest that alexis Mikulski Ruiz is a commerce writer at Penske Media, where she tests, reviews, and writes about the latest in lifestyle, fashion, tech, and entertainment. A lifelong shopaholic, she’s dedicated to helping readers separate the hype from the must-haves. #154339. Mechanical vs magnetic keyboards — and which should you buy?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

Mechanical vs magnetic keyboards — and which should you buy?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I give away a lot of keyboards.
  • One of the main questions I ask people is, "do you want a mechanical keyboard or magnetic keyboard?" And the main response I get is, "what's the difference?".
  • In simple terms, it comes down to whether you're mostly gaming or typing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I give away a lot of keyboards. Sounds weird, I know, but stay with me here. I've reviewed dozens of keyboards. I once had a personal collection of around 40 boards on my wall. I've tested and used probably over a hundred boards, and probably edited the reviews of a hundred. In short, Tom's Guide senior writer Nikita and I test a lot of keyboards. And we have to give them away when we're done.

One of the main questions I ask people is, "do you want a mechanical keyboard or magnetic keyboard?" And the main response I get is, "what's the difference?".

In simple terms, it comes down to whether you're mostly gaming or typing. But like most things in life, the reality is a little more nuanced than that. Here's what you need to know, with a few of my top suggestions sprinkled in along the way.

Sources indicate that the Keychron K2 HE is a magnetic keyboard, with tons of gaming features. But it's gasket mounted, making it extremely comfortable to type on for long periods of time. I should know, as I reviewed it, and I still use it for work on a regular basis as part of my keyboard rotation.

The non-halo version of my beloved NuPhy Halo75 V2, the Node75 ticks many of the same boxes. Beautiful styling, beautiful switches, beautiful keycap profile. I awarded the Node75 a full five stars in my review. It really is that good, especially for the money. And now it's even cheaper.

Recent findings suggest that the main differences come down to whether you need certain gaming features, or whether you want a certain typing feel. However, there are some extra considerations to make... like sound.

Sources indicate that the most compelling reason to buy a magnetic keyboard is for the gaming features. Magnetic switches actuate via magnetic resistance rather than a physical mechanism, so aren't tied down to a single fixed actuation point (i.e. a key depression point where the input is triggered). This opens up a plethora of awesome gaming features that you won't find even on a high-end mechanical gaming keyboard.

There's adjustable actuation, so you can set your keys to actuate with as little as 0.1mm of input. Multiple actuations per keystroke are also possible: you can set the W key so that halfway down is walk, and fully down is actually bound to Shift+W, so run.

And many keyboard manufacturers like Keychron and NuPhy have introduced other cool features that take advantage of magnetic detection, like NuPhy's 'Mod Tap', which changes the input based on how hard/fast you press the key.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Industry observers note that "What about Rapid Trigger?" I hear you call. "And Snap Tap?". I'm gettin' there! 'Rapid Trigger' allows repeat actuations without needing to recycle the switch fully to its reset point — you can basically spam faster. That's not physically possible on a mechanical switch, despite some manufacturers claiming their mechanical keyboards do it.

Last Key Prioritization, A.K.A. 'Snap Tap' is possible on a mechanical keyboard. This is a type of SOCD (simultaneous opposing cardinal direction) resolution. In other words: what the keyboard does when two opposites are inputted at the same time. 'Snap Tap' is just one of a few resolutions to this, and tells the board to prioritize the last key pressed, facilitating quick and easy counter strafing in games with interia-based accuracy penalties like "Valorant" and "Counter-Strike 2" (where it'll get you kicked). You can do this via firmware on a mechanical keyboard.

Industry observers note that that doesn't mean mechanical switches are bad for gaming. Unless you're actually going to use any of the above features, ultra-snappy mechanical switches are perfectly fine for most casual and even some competitive gaming. They just don't offer you all the fancy bells and whistles of their magnetic counterparts.

Now, I've been rather pro-magnetic so far, haven't I. This is where the tables are turned. When it comes to typing experience, at least for now, traditional mechanical switches really have a leg up over magnetic. And it all comes down to how switches feel under your finger.

Mechanical switches offer a much more tactile experience, giving you feedback under your fingers. And I'm not just talking about 'Tactile' switches that have a mechanical bump. Even linear mechanical switches (with no mechanical bump) can give you a feeling different to magnetic switches, because they're typically designed with feel in mind — different weightings, springs and such will all affect how a linear switch feels.

Sources indicate that in short, this makes typing more enjoyable. That remarked, there are some upsides to magnetic switches for typing. Adjustable actuation is the main benefit. You can dial in actuation points to wherever is best for you, which allows you to be as fast and accurate as possible. For example, I make far fewer mistakes at 2.6mm actuation, which in turn increases my type speeds as much as 5-10 words per minute. So I set all magnetic keyboards to 2.6mm when type testing (and usually have a work profile using 2.6mm).

There's a spanner in the works these days, too. Manufacturers are now launching true hybrid keyboards that can hot swap between both mechanical and magnetic switches. While Keychron and Gateron have recently debuted the first (that I know of) tactile magnetic switch, giving the bumpy feel of a traditional mechanical tactile switch but the gaming features of a magnetic one. Up to now, all magnetic switches have been linear and smooth in operation — it's always felt a bit soulless to a tactile mechanical fan.

According to recent reports, for now, though, there's still a much wider array of mechanical switches on offer, with different weights, feels and characteristics. So for typists interested in how their keyboard feels, I'd still recommend mechanical.

According to recent reports, you'll also want to consider some other criteria. Mechanical keyboards designed with typing rather than gaming in mind tend to be more comfortable. They often use gasket mounts (where the PCB, switches and keycaps are suspended on rubber gaskets) which give you a comfy, bouncy feeling under your fingers.

Recent findings suggest that some gaming keyboards, or hybrid boards, use gasket mounts. Typically, though, performance magnetic gaming keyboards will use firmer mounts (top, plate, or tray mounts), which move about less. If your actuation is triggered in 0.1mm increments, you don't want your switches wobbling about.

Industry observers note that similarly, looks aren't really part of this debate, as any keyboard can be styled well or otherwise. Typically, though, custom mechanical keyboards tend to be designed with styling as a prime consideration, and therefore look a little more fun (speaking very generally).

Industry observers note that then, of course, there's sound. With the wider array of switches available on the market, and the fact they're built for the custom enthusiast market, mechanical boards tend to sound better. But there are bland examples found in both genres.

Finally, there's poll rates. But this is a bit of a non-problem. 8K polling is found on both magnetic and mechanical keyboards, but it's mostly snake oil. 1,000Hz found on many mechanical boards is more than enough for low latency gaming and to minimize the chance of missed inputs.

My primary advice here is this: just consider what you actually need. Don't be suckered in by all the marketing talk and fancy features. And don't think price is an issue. You can pick up magnetic and mechanical keyboards for under $50.

According to recent reports, are you going to be doing lots of competitive gaming where you need cutting edge performance features? If so, get a magnetic keyboard.

Industry observers note that do you care about a beautiful experience under your fingers? If so, you can consider a mechanical keyboard with lovely switches, or the ability to hot-swap between them. If you don't care about purist type-feel and just want raw speed and accuracy, a magnetic keyboard might still be best for heavy typists.

According to recent reports, and here's the curve ball. Do you want the best of both? Then invest in a dual MX/HE keyboard, but be prepared to spend big bucks.

The Keychron K2 HE is a magnetic keyboard, with tons of gaming features. But it's gasket mounted, making it extremely comfortable to type on for long periods of time. I should know, as I reviewed it, and I still use it for work on a regular basis as part of my keyboard rotation.

In terms of sheer performance and polish versus cost, the NuPhy Air60 HE is my top Hall Effect gaming keyboard. It's a lot cheaper than the venerated Wooting 60HE+, yet offers just as many features and the companion software, NuPhy.io is (almost) as slick as Wooting's. For the money, though, this would be my pick. If you don't like low-profile, you could also check out the NuPhy FIeld75 HE.

This keyboard is a bit of a shameless rip off of the Wooting 60HE+... even down to the strap accessory. I haven't tested this exact model, but I have tested its bigger sibling, the HE75 Mag, and for under $50, these magnetic boards rule. You won't get the software polish of the Wooting board the HE60 emulates, or indeed of NuPhy or Keychron, but this is a budget pick after all... you can't have everything at this price.

Sources indicate that the non-halo version of my beloved NuPhy Halo75 V2, the Node75 ticks many of the same boxes. Beautiful styling, beautiful switches, beautiful keycap profile. I awarded the Node75 a full five stars in my review. It really is that good, especially for the money. And now it's even cheaper.

In a recent development, the Rainy 75 Pro is probably the best sounding keyboard we've tested. It was so good that, even though my colleague reviewed it, I had to get one for myself. It's an absolute dream to type on too, thanks to the Kailh Cocoa switches.

If you're after a competent all-rounder mechanical board for typing and gaming on a budget, the Keychron C1 Pro 8K is my suggestion. This board is crazy cheap given its performance, switches and styling. The perfect entry-level mechanical board, if you ask me.

Discount with coupon! Remember when I said hybrid MX/HE boards don't come cheap? Yeah, the Lofree Hyzen is about as cheap as they come right now. Your other option is the slightly cheaper Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE, which is a better board and comes with a tactile magnetic switch, but it's still in pre-order until December.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it.

In a recent development, the organization recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed ….

Industry observers note that character․AI had long come under fire for its extremely irresponsible attitude to privacy and safety. Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage users, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The firm filed for bankruptcy last month.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot firm from auctioning off consumers’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […].

Recent findings suggest that “Character․AI’s blueprint to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its people — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta mentioned in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”.

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

It has been revealed that siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

When a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

The data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

Apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization is a 1953 jazz music theory book written by George Russell.
  • Russell believed that dominant function is the driving force behind all harmonic motion.
  • Industry observers note that russell builds a prototype chromatic scale starting on the Lydian Tonic by stacking fifths, skipping the interval between the seventh and eighth tones, and placing the skipped tone at the end for having the lowest level of tonal gravity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization is a 1953 jazz music theory book written by George Russell. The book is the founding text of the Lydian Chromatic Concept (LCC), or Lydian Chromatic Theory (LCT). Russell's work postulates that all music is based on the tonal gravity of the Lydian mode.

Russell believed that dominant function is the driving force behind all harmonic motion. Russell focuses on the Lydian mode because it can be built with fifths. For instance, to construct a C Lydian scale one could list the first seven tones on the circle of fifths starting with C, the desired Lydian Tonic. This process would yield C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯. If these tones are voiced in the space of an octave, they form the Lydian mode; specifically, C Lydian (C, D, E, F♯, G, A, B).[2] Additionally, Russell observed, when these tones are voiced in thirds they form the preferred form of a major 13 (#11) chord.[3].

Industry observers note that russell builds a prototype chromatic scale starting on the Lydian Tonic by stacking fifths, skipping the interval between the seventh and eighth tones, and placing the skipped tone at the end for having the lowest level of tonal gravity. Using C as the Lydian Tonic yields the following 12-note scale with enharmonic respellings: C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯, G♯, E♭ (D♯), B♭ (A♯), F (E♯), D♭ (C♯). Thus the Lydian Chromatic Scale and all its derivatives contain only Pythagorean intervals.[4].

According to recent reports, russell posited that tonal gravity emanates from the first seven tones of the Lydian mode. As the player ventures further from the Lydian tonic however (and further up the circle of fifths), the tonal gravity shifts. For example, if notes further up the circle of fifths (e.g. ♯2/♭3) are used, the tonal gravity is probably shifting.[5].

It has been revealed that russell's theory has had far-reaching effect especially in the realm of modal jazz. Art Farmer said that it "opens the door to countless means of melodic expression"[6] and critic Joachim-Ernst Berendt described it as "the first work deriving a theory of jazz harmony from the immanent laws of jazz" and as "the pathbreaker for Miles Davis's and John Coltrane's 'modality'".[7] Bill Evans and Miles Davis used the theory[8][9] to record modal jazz such as the album Kind of Blue. John Coltrane's modal jazz is usually analyzed using Russell's method.[10] In arguably his most famous piece, "Giant Steps," Coltrane can be heard traveling through a succession of three parent Lydian Chromatic scales: C Lydian, A♭ Lydian, and E Lydian.[11] Additionally, many conservatories teach Russell's theory to varying degrees.[12][13].

Amazon's Black Friday 2026 sale has brought the Sonos Arc Ultra down to $849 from its usual $1,099, a $250 discount that marks its lowest price yet. PCMag named it the best soundbar of 2024 and gave it an “outstanding” rating in its review. Still, $849 is a lot to spend on a single soundbar, and anyone shopping on a tighter budget will find more affordable picks in our Fire TV soundbar roundup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out our comprehensive Black Friday coverage.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to initiative around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a big step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a new Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

It has been revealed that at the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

Recent findings suggest that in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Denis Villeneuve notes he is “deeply disappointed” that Disney chose to release box office juggernaut Avengers: Doomsday over the same December 18 weekend as the third instalment in his Dune franchise.

Sources indicate that in a new interview with Time Magazine, Villeneuve said his first two Dune films had to contend with the tail end of the pandemic and then the Hollywood strikes, respectively, something he described as “rough” and “not easy”. With the third film, he thought he and Warner Bros were out of the woods. Then came news that Disney was dropping into the same release weekend with Avengers. Related Stories News 'Avengers: Doomsday' U.S. Presales Now At $100M+ As Pic Heads For $270M+ Opening - Box Office News Chris Evans On Secret Meetings About 'Avengers' Return Despite Saying He Was "Happily Retired" From MCU.

Sources indicate that he expanded: “Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth. So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”” Watch on Deadline.

According to recent reports, my colleague Anthony had a report earlier this week looking at both films’ domestic box office outlook. NRG tracking has Avengers gunning for a $270M+ start with a shot at $300M and Dune eyeing a $75M-80M start. The former is NRG’s biggest ever opening weekend projection. The latter would be close to Dune: Part Two‘s first domestic weekend.

It has been revealed that the Time interview also touched on Villeneuve’s upcoming James Bond film. Villeneuve described his excitement for it: “I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this fresh project. It is so different.“.

Sources indicate that the filmmaker was asked whether he would stick to tradition or look to deviate with his Bond: “I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.”.

The director and interviewer were speaking ahead of the news that Robert Pattinson will be Bond, but Villeneuve acknowledged that whoever they chose wouldn’t please everyone:.

In a recent development, “No matter what we do, we will never please everybody. When Daniel Craig was cast, it was a sh-tstorm. He was blond. He was short. He was not seen as an action hero. Yet when we talk about James Bond today it is because of Daniel Craig’s extraordinary interpretation. And that was a different environment in 2006 before social media. I expect a hurricane when we bring our choice to the world. Some people will be happy. Some will be mad. I can do nothing about that. At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen. Then they will be able to judge.“.

AI made self-hosting fun again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 155 min read (31009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Janlukas

⏱️ ~155 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been self-hosting things for many years.
  • I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things.
  • Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a significant reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a major reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting challenges. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, enhancement, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of fresh releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security complications, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more key than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by major tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

According to recent reports, AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, patch, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server.
