Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security challenges, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by substantial tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

It has been revealed that of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or patch a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely fresh machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Sources indicate that previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security problems, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more crucial than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something fresh is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by massive tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

According to recent reports, skincare is far from just a trending topic on your TikTok or Instagram feeds; it’s a billion-dollar industry. From facial cleansers to cosmetic treatments and procedures, such as Botox injections, there are seemingly endless routes to the same thing: Clear and young-looking skin. That’s not even including apps like Facetune and various filters we can apply to our photos to hide even the suggestion of aging. In our society, getting older is taboo; something we may silently acknowledge as inevitable yet not really discuss, all the while doing anything and everything to “prevent” it from happening at all.

The truth is, there is no magic cure for aging. Try as you might, even the most knowledgeable skincare experts have yet to come up with a way to keep time from marching across our faces. That said, that doesn’t mean you can’t age gracefully, or that you have to completely empty your wallet to do so. By taking proper steps to care for your skin, you can not only ensure that it remains healthy throughout your life, but also slow down the effects of aging. One method is showing promising results: red light therapy.

It has been revealed that red light therapy has been clinically studied and shown to improve your skin’s overall appearance, helping combat wrinkles, scars, acne, and other signs of aging. To understand how it works, we must first understand why things like wrinkles appear in the first place.

“As we age, our cells become larger. This makes it harder for them to divide and multiply, which slows our bodies’ ability to regenerate,” says Shane Miller, a licensed esthetician and the owner of the popular Instagram account @howtohydrate.

According to recent reports, that’s where red light therapy devices come in; these devices come in different forms, sometimes as masks you can wear on your face, and other times as panels you can hang and stand in front of. These red light panels administer low-wavelength red light to stimulate our skin cells, giving them the energy they need to continue the upkeep of our skin’s appearance and texture.

Regularly using red light therapy panels in moderation may help maintain a healthy sheen and improve any fine lines or wrinkles, as well as reduce inflammation that may appear as a result of conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, and contact dermatitis.

Miller recommends using your red light therapy device daily on a freshly cleaned and dry face, before you’ve applied any serums, moisturizers, and/or sunscreen if you’re using it during the day. Unlike UVA/UVB rays, red light does not pose a threat to your skin. However, it’s always a good idea to proceed with caution when introducing a newly introduced step into your routine, as everyone’s skin is different. Be sure to consult the instructions on any device, protect your eyes, and consult a dermatologist before use if you have any light sensitivities.

If you’re unsure of how to integrate red light therapy into your daily routine, Miller recommends consulting with a licensed esthetician or a dermatologist to see if it’s right for you.

The wavelength is adjustable between six settings, letting you target different benefits. Thanks to its size (65 inches tall), you won’t need to reposition during sessions, and it can be tilted to use horizontally.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo.
  • According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599).
  • According to recent reports, unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo.

According to recent reports, unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

Sources indicate that there are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is right now on sale with a starting price of $999.

For that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

The MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

Recent findings suggest that as I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

The M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

One of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

In a recent development, to recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

Industry observers note that beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

Industry observers note that what do you think of the MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air decision? Which would you choose? Let us know down in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in a pretty funny format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their consumers.

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

It has been revealed that instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Customers We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

According to recent reports, shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.

Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.

I'm not affiliated with OpenAI and this may indeed be a viral marketing idea they're testing. But I had such a laugh, I figured others would have some fun with it as well and decided to share it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chinese director Zou Jing’s A Girl Unknown won the top $75,000 Best Narrative prize at the Doha Film Festival as the second edition of its revamped format came to a close on Friday evening.

The China-set first feature follows the fate of a young girl who is found abandoned as a baby in a rubbish bin and then grows up from babyhood through to adolescence with three sets of different guardians and circumstances.

It has been revealed that the film world premiered in Cannes Critics’ Week earlier this year where it won the Fipresci Prize. The picture was acquired for the U.S. by Greenwich Entertainment which is planning an early 2027 tour and release. Related Stories News International Insider: Doha Days; Tricky Week For BAFTA; 'Remarried Empress' Interview News Todd Boehly Dissects How Daniel Katz's Trading Desk Acumen Fed Into A24 Success: "Very Few Entertainment People Understand Math".

It has been revealed that rafael Manuel won Best Artistic Achievement in Narrative for Filipiñana about a 17-year-old girl who discovers a rotten side to the posh countryclub where she works on the golf course. The film world premiered in Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Special Jury Award. The film is the Philippines’ entry for the 99th Academy Awards. Watch on Deadline.

Best Actress was awarded posthumously to Josette Kwanya for her performance in her son Auguste Bernard Kouemo’s House of the Wind as an elderly Cameroonian woman waiting for her children to return home after they left for Europe in search of fresh life opportunities.

The film won Venice’s Lion of the Future for a Debut Film when it premiered there in its Orizzonti sidebar in September.

This year’s jury was presided over by Japanese director Naomi Kawase, who was joined by by Oscar-winning documentarian Gianfranco Rosi, rising actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha and Palestinian director Kamal Aljafari.

In further prizes, Best Documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land about a Bedouin family struggling to preserve their traditional way of life in tents, as well as the Fipresci prize, which is being awarded at the festival for the first time this year.

In other documentary prizes, Tala Hadid’s Bardi won the Best Artistic Achievement for Documentary.

Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, Festival Director and CEO of Doha Film Institute noted the 2026 Doha Film Festival tapped into her institute’s belief in “the power of stories to transcend borders, challenge perspectives and bring the experiences of people and communities into the global conversation.”.

“At Doha Film Institute, we believe that important voices deserve to be seen, heard and recognised. Doha Film Festival exists to provide that platform, bringing together filmmakers and audiences from across the world, championing bold and independent storytelling, and creating space for stories that might otherwise go untold,” she said.

“The films we honour tonight remind us that cinema is not simply a reflection of the world we live in; it is a force that can shape how we understand it, connect with one another and imagine a more empathetic future.”.

States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

📖 0% read

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Commonwealth of Virginia Office of the Attorney General.

202 North 9th Street Richmond, Virginia 23219 804-786-2071 FAX 804-786-1991 Virginia Relay Service 800-828-1120.

For media inquiries only, contact:   Rae Pickett RPickett@oag.state.va.us.

Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Firm of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform  Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant newly introduced protections for consumers.

***Read the full filing here***.

RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.

In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence manufacturer, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.

According to recent reports, “This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” noted Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”.

In a recent development, with a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable.

Industry observers note that the company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.

“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” stated Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”.

In a recent development, in his filing, Attorney General Jones demonstrates that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.

A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs.

It has been revealed that spaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent.

Recent findings suggest that “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold major tech accountable when they break the law.”.

“Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield.

Industry observers note that attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court.

According to recent reports, amazon has dropped the price of the two-pack Netgear Orbi 770 Series Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System to $449.99 from $549.99, saving you $100 on a setup that includes a router and a satellite node, with a combined coverage area of up to 5,500 square feet. If you don't need quite as much coverage, smaller configurations, including a single satellite node, is also discounted as part of Amazon's early Black Friday sale. It now costs $239.99, down from $349.99, and covers up to 2,750 square feet.

According to recent reports, the system uses tri-band Wi-Fi 7 technology to spread your connection across three bands, with combined speeds of up to 11,000Mbps. It also supports wider 320MHz channels, though you'll need compatible Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of those faster connections. If you prefer wired connections for devices that need a more stable link, the main router has three 2.5GbE LAN ports and a 2.5GbE WAN port, while the satellite offers two 2.5GbE LAN ports. This gives you plenty of room to connect a gaming console, desktop PC, or smart TV, and you can also use wired backhaul if your home has Ethernet cabling.

Once everything is connected, you can handle setup and day-to-day management through Netgear's Orbi app, while a web dashboard offers additional settings (for anyone who wants more control over their network), including VPN access and port forwarding, notes this PCMag review. There's no USB connectivity or 10GbE support, and some of its more advanced security and parental control features require a separate subscription after a free 30-day trial. Its Smart Parental Controls, for instance, cost $7.99 per month or $69.99 annually.

On today’s Crew Call we chat with near EGOT winner David Byrne about “Let Me Sell You A Dream,” his upcoming song for Alex Gibney’s controversial documentary Musk about, yes, Elon Musk.

Byrne tells us about co-writing the ditty during the European leg of his latest tour “Who is the Sky?” and biking to a London musical equipment shop to get recording gear, so he could create a makeshift studio in his hotel room and lay down tracks for Oscar nominated composer Daniel Pemberton, who is a co-writer on the song.

In recording the tune, Byrne exclaims, “I’d sit at my little mic stand in a hotel room and I’d go into character as Elon Musk (exhale), and just start ranting.” Related Stories News 'American Psycho' Gets Axed: Luca Guadagnino Confirms His Adaptation Is "Not Happening" News 'Artificial' Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino On Whether AI Is Humanity's Doomsday & Sam Altman's Arsenal - Crew Call Podcast.

Off the bat, “Let Me Sell You a Dream” in its fast dance tempo brings to mind the 1986 Talking Heads single “Wild Wild Life” which Byrne wrote for the Warner Bros absurdist reality movie he directed and co-wrote, True Stories. Watch on Deadline.

It has been revealed that byrne indicates that “Let Me Sell You a Dream” had to be “hard hitting…It’s going to have an impact at the at the end. It has to jump right in, and grab you by the throat.”.

“It’s not one of those fading-while-the-credits roll and everybody decides, ‘I’m going to get up, get out and get back to my car before everybody else.'”.

According to recent reports, “Let Me Sell You a Dream” is also throwback to the types of pseudo anti-yuppie tunes that Talking Heads was known for including 1988’s “(Nothing) But Flowers” and 1979’s “Life During Wartime”. Byrne explains that the Musk end-credits song was arguably the “fastest” he has ever written in his career. To date, while Musk has railed against Gibney about the documentary, he hasn’t sent any praise or tomatoes to the Oscar winning Byrne. Give a listen to Byrne’s process here:.

Byrne also takes us down memory regaling that his first instrument was a violin, and how he grew up inspired by The Rolling Stones and Motown. He also chats about the early days of the Talking Heads when they were discovered by Sire Records’ boss Seymour Stein (“He could meet with us, talk with us and and sing ours songs back to us”) as well as working with Bernardo Bertolucci and producer Jeremy Thomas on the score for The Last Emperor which won Byrne an original score Oscar which he co-shared with Cong Su and Ryūichi Sakamoto.

A time when Byrne was told by the music industry he was too audacious? How about when he did his first solo album in 1989, the Latino infused “Rei Momo”?

“They implied that I shot myself in the foot and that the fans were going to leave,” mentioned Byrne, which if you look at the full houses for his concerts, not to mention the Broadway run of his concert show American Utopia is definitely not the case: His appearance last November at the Dolby Theater drew the likes of Oliver Stone, Judd Apatow and Derek Waters, while his Hollywood Bowl late August appearances for “Who Is The Sky?” were jam packed.

“I thought that if I keep trying different things, you’re not going to get pigeonholed as being the blues rock band or the funk band,” Byrne shares, “I thought if I can do different things, that’s going to give you wiggle room, and allow you to do different things down the road and hopefully the audience goes with you.”.

And of course, we ask the never-ending question to Byrne, that even after a great reunion with the Talking Heads for the A24 Imax 2023 re-release of seminal concert film Stop Making Sense, will they ever tour together again?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nobody keeps a schedule like a touring artist. Red-eyes, soundchecks, 2 a.m. sets, and a call time the next morning that doesn’t care how late the show ran. Fans see the stage, but the real work is keeping your body ready to do it all again tomorrow.

David Beckham has lived his own version of that life for 30 years, from the soccer pitch, to fashion weeks, global campaigns, and co-owning Inter Miami CF.

“I’ve often felt overwhelmed by how many different products it takes to truly support your body,” the sporting icon indicates. So he co-founded IM8 with health sciences company Prenetics, and the brand’s most complete product now carries his name: the Beckham Stack.

The Beckham Stack pairs two products. Daily Ultimate Essentials Pro packs 90+ ingredients across 16 supplement categories, and Daily Ultimate Longevity adds 10 compounds for long-term cellular health, including 600 mg of NMN.

Together, they cover what a demanding schedule wears down. You get 100 mg CoQ10 and B vitamins for energy, 30 mg saffron extract and choline for focus and sleep, and 2,500 mg of electrolytes to rehydrate after a night on stage or a long flight. Ten billion CFU probiotics and digestive enzymes support a gut that has been through three time zones and too much catering, while vitamin C, zinc, selenium, elderberry, and reishi round out immune support for the days you are shaking hands with a newly introduced city every night.¹.

According to recent reports, the co-owner list reads like a festival lineup. IM8’s shareholders include Diplo, Lily Collins, Jay Shetty, NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo and tennis star Aryna Sabalenka, all of whom are co-owners through Prenetics. The brand is also the Official Health Supplements Partner of Inter Miami CF.

In a recent development, the star power comes with serious science too. IM8’s Scientific Advisory Board includes Dr. Dawn Mussallem of Mayo Clinic, former NASA Chief Scientist Dr. James L. Green and Prof. Suzanne Devkota of Cedars-Sinai.

In a 12-week randomized controlled trial of IM8’s Daily Ultimate Essentials formula, 95% of participants reported more energy, 85% reported less bloating, 80% reported better sleep and 75% reported sharper focus.² Essentials Pro is also NSF Certified for Sport, and IM8 holds a 4.5 out of 5 rating on Trustpilot based on more than 2,000 reviews.

Each product comes in a single-serve sachet that fits in a carry-on, a tour bus bunk, or a back pocket. Tear both open, mix with water, and your routine is done in about a minute. Flavors include Açaí + Mixed Berries, Mango Passion Fruit, and Lemon + Orange, all sweetened with fermented sugarcane instead of stevia.

The Beckham Stack is $139 per month on a quarterly subscription, compared with $261 for a one-time purchase. IM8 estimates the same ingredients bought as separate supplements would run about $502 per month.

Quarterly looks include a 90-day money-back guarantee and free shipping, HSA/FSA payments are accepted for eligible customers, and you can pause or cancel anytime.

Judge orders Apple to produce 3,200 documents in Epic Games dispute

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, following Epic’s allegations that Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • With Apple and Epic trading arguments in the Supreme Court over whether the civil contempt ruling against Apple should stand, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • In a recent development, in August, Apple submitted its proposal to the district court, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, following Epic’s allegations that Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

With Apple and Epic trading arguments in the Supreme Court over whether the civil contempt ruling against Apple should stand, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

In a recent development, in August, Apple submitted its proposal to the district court, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%. Epic, however, is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

Earlier this month, Epic accused Apple of improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching a set of search terms agreed upon by both companies to help identify documents that could shed light on how Apple arrived at those rates.

Recent findings suggest that […] Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple claims decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness.

Apple, in turn, pushed back against Epic’s accusations, saying the search terms were overly broad and had captured large numbers of documents unrelated to the proceedings.

[…] at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms […]. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The tech giant also asked the court to reject Epic’s motion to order it to produce all non-privileged documents matching the agreed-upon search terms, and alternatively suggested submitting a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deemed nonresponsive to a Special Master for independent review.

As it turns out, neither manufacturer got exactly what it originally wanted, but the judge ruled largely in Epic’s favor on how to determine whether Apple had improperly withheld documents.

Following a hearing in which both companies presented their respective proposals for how a randomized sampling of the documents should be conducted, Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson decided to adopt Epic’s proposal, which called for Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents it had previously deemed nonresponsive, along with their associated document families, for Epic itself to review.

All documents in the sample will be drawn from the files of the seven Apple custodians referenced in Epic’s original motion.

Apple, by contrast, had suggested a considerably smaller sample of 383 documents, arguing that this would be statistically significant at a 95% confidence level.

In his decision, Judge Hixson agreed that Epic had legitimate reasons to question Apple’s reasons for withholding the documents:.

In a recent development, apple’s responsiveness rate is so dramatically low that it raises red flags. With Apple screening out more than 99% of the documents that hit on the agreed search terms, it is unreasonable to ask Epic to believe that Apple is making these responsiveness calls in good faith. That is particularly true in this case, in which Judge Gonzalez Rogers has sanctioned Apple for its large-scale abuse of the attorney-client privilege for the purpose of obscuring the evidence.

Judge Hixson also rejected Apple’s suggestion that a Special Master conduct the review, arguing that given the level of familiarity with the case required to assess the relevance of these documents, Epic was the only practical option for determining whether Apple had systematically misclassified them.

Realistically, the only person who has the practical ability to determine if Apple has been systematically mis-coding documents as nonresponsive is its opponent, Epic.

In his decision, the judge agreed with Apple that the manufacturer should be allowed to review the documents for privileged and sensitive information before producing them to Epic, and authorized Apple to designate all documents produced as part of the exercise as Attorneys’ Eyes Only.

Importantly, Judge Hixson has not yet determined whether Apple systematically misclassified responsive documents as nonresponsive, nor has he imposed the daily monetary sanctions originally requested by Epic.

Apple now has until December 8 to complete the document production, with Epic having until December 15 to file any objections, and Apple until December 22 to respond.

Thursday was a dual celebration for Justin Timberlake‘s visit with Jimmy Fallon on NBC’s Tonight Show: There was Thanksgiving, of course, which you can see in the photo above was most certainly not ignored by the two old friends, and then for the former boy bander the visit was an opportunity to celebrate the 20th anniversary of his album FutureSex/LoveSounds.

And of course there’s always newly introduced material to plug, and last night it was Timberlake‘s four-part doc series streaming on Apple TV beginning December 11.

The Thanksgiving visit began with Timberlake joining Fallon in a musical number celebrating “The History of Party Songs.” With Timberlake initially putting up some mock reluctance, the two then released into Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” then proceeded through a smorgasbord of classic dance hits, including Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body,” Wild Cherry’s “Play That Funky Music White Boy,” “Good Times” by Chic, Cool and the Gang’s “Celebration,” and some others you might be able catch before the major finish of The Backstreet Boys’ “I Want It That Way.” Related Stories News Ariana Grande Crashes Jimmy Fallon's Monologue With 'Focker-In-Law's Ben Stiller & Robert De Niro Late Night TV 'Tonight Show': Jimmy Fallon & Jamie Lee Curtis Channel Fielder & Holmes In Cold Open.

Watch the musical medley here: Watch on Deadline.

Timberlake also reflected on the making of the FutureSex/LoveSounds album, noting that at the time of its recording he’d been listening to “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics, INXS…but we were kind of thinking, How we can take the sonics of dance music and flip it?”.

Timberlake recalls that, as presented in the upcoming docuseries, his record label at the time was not initially impressed with the album, thinking it was “too fast,” to which Timberlake responded, “That’s why it’s going to work.” He also remembered that the label was disappointed that he wasn’t using his signature falsetto enough. “I was listening to [David Bowie’s] ‘Rebel Rebel’ a lot…and that music at that time sounded so daring.” Timberlake says he wanted to create the impression that the singer was a character in the song, as Bowie so often did, and the result was “SexyBack.”.

It has been revealed that regarding the upcoming four-part Timberlake documentary series, the singer explained that he overcame his initial reluctance – “I’m sort of famously private” – by trusting director and friend Fisher Stevens. “I feel like I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that made me a better human,” he noted.

“But the more we sat down and talked, the more I found myself searching for something that was beneath the surface a little more,” he continued. “And I think that at the end of the day I sort of mustered up some courage to talk about things that I’ve never talked about before. Things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”.

Sources indicate that timberlake also paid tribute to the late singer-songwriter D’Angelo, the major influence who died October 14, 2025. “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything,” Timberlake told Fallon. “You know, he was one of those artists. Rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”.

And finally, here’s Timberlake’s performance that capped the Fallon appearance, taking place at Fresh York’s famed Rainbow Room atop 30 Rock. He performs a medley of “FutureSex/LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.”.

The docuseries Timberlake airs on Apple TV on Friday, December 11 with the first two episodes, followed by the third episode on Friday, December 18 and the finale on Wednesday, December 23, 2026.

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar indicates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that be sure to read to the end for what I can guarantee is the most exciting and cinematric R package bibliography youâve ever seen. Everything you see in the below blog post was rendered in R with the rayverse.

Industry observers note that eight years ago, rayshader started as a small experiment in making beautiful maps in R. The first version was based on a simple question: what if we combined raytracing and cartography? I had always been interested in learning both about mapping and pathtracing, and what better way than to combine the two ideas into a single R package? The massive âaha!â moment came when I applied that method with interactive 3D terrain for the first time and took it for a spin.

Recent findings suggest that the surface was no longer just a shaded map: it felt tangible and real, a 3D rectangle twirling like a Little Debbie cosmic brownie on a microwave turntable. The combination of cartographic hillshading and 3D raytraced terrain looked spectacular in a way that, at the time, mostly lived in bespoke Blender scenes or other advanced 3D modeling tools. And unlike Blender, you didnât need to learn a whole latest ecosystem to visualize your data in 3D: it lived in the same place your data did (R!), which allowed for a gentler learning curve.

But as time went on and the package and userbase expanded, I had a nagging feeling: rayshader was still too hard.

It has been revealed that not always, of course: plenty of people were using it, quite effectively. Simple use cases were fine: pass in a matrix, add a few layers, call plot_3d(), and suddenly you had a cool-looking 3D landscape. If thatâs all you needed: great! But if the story you were trying to tell was about data within the landscapeâwell, thatâs where the friction began to burn.

According to recent reports, I built rayshader for people who wanted to make data beautiful without leaving R. Beauty has a real purpose in the world: it draws peopleâs eyes. It doesnât matter how accurate or well-constructed your map is if the reader swipes on by: in the market for human attention, beauty and form are table stakes.

Journalists understood that swiftly, and were some of rayshaderâs earliest adopters.

Recent findings suggest that the Wall Street Journalâs The Future of Arctic Shipping used detailed shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data to explain the complexities of the Northern Sea Route. The piece was recognized by the Information is Beautiful Awards, which described it as a deeply researched story built from shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data. It appeared only a few months after I released rayshader: talk about an introduction! Bloombergâs 2024 Gaza rebuilding story, Gaza Reduced to 42 Million Tonnes of Rubble. What Will It Take to Rebuild?, used R, rayshader, and rayrender as part of the visual system for communicating the scale of destruction and debris in Gaza. And in June 2022, a rayshader 3D flood visualization appeared on the front page of The Sydney Morning Herald, inset into coverage of the Lismore flooding.

That last one stuck with me (and not only because a rayshader map was featured âabove the foldâ in a major newspaper!). Rayshader had started as a way to make beautiful data visualizations in R, but here it was being used in deadline journalism to help explain a disaster to a general audience. The package had left the domain of âfun engaging social media postsâ and entered the visual language of public-interest reporting.

In a recent development, but getting a reader to stop scrolling is only half the problem. Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product. A newsroom deadline is a very good detector of bad API design. If adding buildings takes half a day of coordinate fiddling, that feature might as well not exist. If a 3D path requires a hand-rolled coordinate transform pipeline, nobody is doing that 30 minutes before a deadline. If a pathtraced render looks great but takes too long to converge, it is not going to make it to print. Especially if the editor needs a slight tweak: âOh, sureâjust give me 8 hours to re-render the animation.â Ha. Nope.

Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product.

Recent findings suggest that the problem wasnât so much with rayshader itself: it was how much spatial bookkeeping and manual fiddling you had to do to get data into rayshader before you could do all the fun stuff. And at the root of all that bookkeeping was the humble matrix, rayshaderâs original choice for representing terrain.

Rayshader used matrices to represent terrain because it simplified a lot of the work that went into turning a bunch of elevation values in a 3D object. But most real data does not arrive nicely packaged as a plain rectangular numeric array. It arrives as georeferenced rasters, polygons, lines, and points. It arrives cloaked in an unknown coordinate reference system. It arrives in meters, feet, yards, degrees, or German legal metres. Choosing the matrix as the base input made it easy for me, the developer, by putting the spatial problem (mostly) on the user.

Convert the raster to a matrix. Save the extent. Transform the vector data. Save the CRS. Crop the linework. Pass the heightmap again. Pass the extent again. Wait, is the extent format lat/long/lat/long or lat/lat/long/long? I never rememberâwhatever, try both. The first choice is (somehow!) always wrong. Pass zscale again. Resize the overlay. Pass the CRS again. Check whether the map is oriented correctly. No? Surprise! Errant minus sign. Yuck.

This was not just annoying for beginners. It annoyed me, and I wrote the damn thing: now thatâs a usability red flag! The new version of rayshader includes a series of changes that gets rid of all of this overhead and allows you to focus on presentation instead of the data processing.

In a recent development, the substantial change in rayshader 1.0 is this: rayshader no longer has short-term amnesia. Rayshader now keeps track of all the spatial details from your underlying map so you donât have to worry about it any more.

This changes the user experience from:.

Transform and pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.

Transform and Pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.

The black diamond learning curve is now a gentle bunny slope. Terrain can stay a spatial raster. Road can stay a spatial line and will automatically be converted to the correct coordinate system when plotting. Buildings can be passed in as spatial polygons and will automatically be cropped to the underlying mapâs extent.

In a recent development, A rayshader scene now extracts and caches the crucial metadata from the input data: heightmap, extent, CRS, zscale, vertical exaggeration, and rendered-object metadata. That cache lets downstream render_*() calls do the thing customers always wanted them to do: simply drop data into the scene.

Recent findings suggest that most of the functions can now add to the scene simply by passing the data, plus an optional argument that specifies altitude or height, either directly or through a column in an sf object. The rest of the arguments then focus on how you want to style the data.

It has been revealed that for example, letâs load in some road and elevation data and see what the new API looks like. The code below defines the helpers and loads the data into R. Thereâs no rayshader in it, so you have absolutely no obligation to read it :).

According to recent reports, pretty straightforwardâ¦ just kidding, loading geospatial data is always a pain. Nothing I can do about that! But the real question is: how complex is visualizating all this data once itâs loaded?

Not complex at all! You call the function named after the type of dataâ¦ and it renders the data in the scene. Any additional arguments are just for styling the data to your liking.

According to recent reports, and the payoff is not just less typing: it lets us get to the fun part of 3D data visualization faster. The coolest part of rayshader has always been building strikingly beautiful 3D landscapes from your data. But the third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set. When every point, path, and polygon needs the user to track the CRS and extent info themselves and transform the data appropriately, many users never get to the stage where they can experiment with lighting and composition, styling the data (costume design!), or focus on editing the overall narrative.

The third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set.

Recent findings suggest that this release automates almost all of the behind-the-scenes work. The boring partsâCRS juggling, extent passing, heightmap repetition, matrix conversion, and other bookkeepingâstay in the package internals. The user is then free to jump to the enjoyable creative roles: the executive producer of the analysis, the production designer of the world, or the sound designer of a multi-sensory data experience.

Rayshader now accepts many more spatial inputs for the heightmap. The plot_3d() function can now accept a heightmap as a matrix, a terra::SpatRaster, a raster object, or a raster filename. When the input is spatial, rayshader extracts and caches the extent and CRS. If zscale is not supplied, rayshader derives it from raster cell resolution. If the raster is geographic longitude/latitude, rayshader estimates the meter-per-cell scale at the raster center. The data was always there; it just had to be piped around to the right place! Now I do the plumbing for you.

Recent findings suggest that letâs look at an example. The same DEM and main-road data feed both versions below. The difference is whoâs now doing the spatial bookkeeping (hint: itâs not you).

Internally, rayshader still converts the raster to something it can render. Externally, the scene remembers enough to let the render_*() functions just work.

There is now also a cleaner division between physical scale and visual exaggeration. zscale now describes the relationship between horizontal and vertical units, while vertical_exaggeration describes the stylistic exaggeration. For spatial rasters, rayshader can derive zscale from the raster itself, placing the data at its physical scale. You can then adjust vertical_exaggeration to emphasize the terrain without changing the underlying unit conversion.

And this spatial data directionality can now be reversed. spatialize_image() turns a rayshader image, matrix, RGB array, or RGBA array back into a georeferenced terra::SpatRaster. It can inherit the cached extent and CRS from the active scene, convert rayshaderâs linear color values to sRGB, and optionally append the source heightmap as an additional raster layer. So rayshaderâs output can now feed back into other GIS software, rather than just assume rayshader is the final destination itself.

In a recent development, this release lets rayshader fit into a real spatial workflow: spatial input, then rayshader styling, followed by spatial output. So you can generate beautiful hillshades and terrains in R, and then bring them into other spatial software like QGIS or ArcGIS. Work in the GIS interface you already know, render the terrain in R, and drop the result right back into your map.

It has been revealed that rayshaderâs water was always a bit of an afterthought: it was good for rendering an ocean with bathymetry data, but it didnât really work if the water was localized to one portion of the map. A lake halfway up a mountain shouldnât require flooding everything below it to see the water, but rayshaderâs old water meshing method assumed one water level for the whole map. Which was perfect if all you needed was that one large body of water: set a level and fill the scene to that height. Separate lakes, reservoirs at different elevations, and imperfect shorelines called for something more flexible.

Sources indicate that now water can arrive as a raster or a polygon, high in the mountains or below sea level. render_water() uses the terrain and coordinates already stored in the scene to properly place and render the water in a sane way.

Water can follow grid cells with water_render_method = "raster" or preserve polygon boundaries with the default, water_render_method = "polygon". Both draw a watertight mesh at the footprint and elevation you supply, even when that means an exposed vertical water wall where the supplied shoreline doesnât quite meet the terrain. Fast, flexible, and suitable for the rare case where you need to visualize Moses crossing the Red Sea.

Another (much cooler, IMO) option is water_render_method = "optimized". It fits a closed shoreline to the actual 3D terrain mesh, adjusting the water elevation to match the supplied area. Using the elevations beneath your water footprint to seed candidate levels, the optimizer searches for a contour that comes as close as possible to the supplied water area without spilling out of the terrain. The animation below highlights how candidate levels change the flooded area.

If no closed water body is possibleâfor example, the supplied water would flood the entire mapârayshader falls back to raster water.

In a recent development, A different problem arises when a DEM has no bathymetry: the lake bed and its surface occupy the same plane. shift_terrain() is a new function that can lower the terrain beneath a lake polygon before you add water, making room for the lake instead of letting the surfaces overlap. It can also raise terrain SimCity 2000-style (no tornados or alien invasionsâ¦ yet).

It has been revealed that additionally, in render_highquality(), water can now use a rough dielectric material to spread reflections into the broad highlights you expect from a rippled lake. A perfectly smooth dielectric surface behaves like glass: reflected light stays coherent, so lakes and rivers can turn into polished sheets. Real water has small wind-driven ripples, each reflecting light in a slightly different direction. The microfacet material models this give a more realistic appearance to bodies of water, especially when viewed at a low angle.

In a recent development, streams need to follow the terrain as they wind downhill. render_streams() takes spatial line data, samples the elevation along each path, and builds ribbons of water that hug the surface. Widths can vary by feature, and connected streams can be merged to reduce visible seams in high-quality renders. Put those streams together with lakes and you have a hydrologic scene driven by data.

According to recent reports, note that thereâs no complex GIS concepts on the rayshader side: all the complexity is related to defining the visual style and appearance. As it should beârayshader is a visualization package! The remaining complexity is just standard data complexity present in any analysis: get the data loaded, cleaned, and in a form that represents the thing you care about.

3D maps might seem like a fun little toy rather than a serious class of data visualization, but the third dimension is often surprisingly vital for understanding geospatial data. This becomes less surprising when you realize that the most common mapping tool used by regular peopleâGPS appsâuse 3D quite extensively. When youâre traveling through a city, buildings give you landmarks to match to your surroundings; on a walking or cycling route, the terrain reveals where youâll be climbing; and at a complex highway interchange, seeing which roads pass over one another helps you follow the right ramp and choose the right exit.

Industry observers note that I already had surface-hugging polygons working for streams. Swap the water for asphalt and thereâs a road! Easy, peasy, right?

According to recent reports, no! Whatâs the matter? Weâre spoiled with our GPS apps: weâre used to roads looking like roads. A strip of grey asphalt needs lane markings for someone to know itâs a road. With the help of some fun repeating UV coordinate tricks and our new spatial-first workflow, we can paint properly-sized lines on the road at the cost of a few small textures. And we can use the lane counts supplied in OpenStreetMap data to add the correct number of lanes to each road. Rayshader uses those counts to mesh and texture the road, while the sceneâs spatial information keeps the markings correctly sized.

Sources indicate that in Figure 11, each dash is 10 feet long and each gap is 30 feet. Those familiar markings do double duty: they improve the picture and act as little scale bars scattered through the scene. Beautiful! Pack it up, put a bow on it, and move on to the next feature, right?

According to recent reports, no! Our roads are still smooshed together on one layer. At an interchange, that borders on uninterpretable.

It has been revealed that openStreetMap doesnât provide a full 3D road model. But it does carry one tiny (but extremely useful!) nugget of vertical information needed to draw roads correctly in 2D: drawing order. Draw layer 0, then layer 1, then layer 2, and the right road appears on top. That tells us which road crosses over which; it doesnât tell us their heights or how the ramps return to ground level. Is this enough information to fully reconstruct our 3D roads?

The tempting shortcut is to turn each layer into a fixed height: find the crossings, lift each road by a standard overpass height, and ease it back toward the ground with some sort of ad hoc relaxation rule. What could go wrong?

It has been revealed that everything. Everything can go wrong.

Recent findings suggest that simple hacks? Donât work here. Turns out the world is filled with little annoying complications like a bridge crossing a sunken highway (the highway is already below ground, so the bridge needs no change in elevation), or short segments in interchanges that are technically not stacked but fall between stacked layers, or places where the road is technically stacked over a traversable water body (which also counts as a layer!), or a thousand other pesky little details.

It has been revealed that what are we to do then? How can we implement realistic highways? Itâs not like thereâs a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3Dâwait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?

It has been revealed that the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) has a design manual for Interstate highways. Two of the things it covers are exactly what our map is missing. How much room does a truck need under a bridge? How steep can the road get on its way up there? Now that rayshader knows the scale of the scene, I can give the solver a clearance in feet and a maximum grade in percent. Here are the default settings I gave the road solver (these are customizable):.

According to recent reports, we can turn these requirements into constraints on the road heights. While the rules arenât guaranteed to generate roads that match the real-world roads exactly, itâs going to be pretty close: excursions from the bare minimum allowable ruleset will usually only increase cost, and weâre talking government contracts here. Around each interchange, we discretize the roads into short segments and solve for their elevations together: maintain the crossing order and clearance, limit the grades, and keep the roads close to the terrain wherever possible.

Recent findings suggest that itâs not like thereâs a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3Dâwait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?

For example, a road can weave over and under several others. Lifting one crossing changes the grades leading into the next, so solving each crossing independently wonât workâwe have to solve all the linked constraints at once. We build a graph of the road connections with {igraph}, locate crossings with {sf}, and follow the constraints along connected road segments. Each connected optimization region gets a sparse quadratic problem, assembled with {Matrix} and solved with {osqp}. It turns out, R has everything you need to build and optimize road profiles.

It has been revealed that itâs pretty cool how closely a set of road-design rules and OSMâs layer ordering can recreate a complex interchange. The layer tags tell us which road goes over which, and the rules guide how the ramps connect them. Hereâs Houston, now modeled in a sane way:.

In a recent development, beautiful. And since I went to Houston for this yearâs Posit::conf, I was able to drive over specific intersections I rendered here and confirm that yes: the roads were accurately meshed. Minus the traffic.

According to recent reports, the novelty seeking half of my brain immediately followed this thought with: âYou should put in cars now!â to which the logical, killjoy side of my brain responded âNO! STOP IT! YOUâVE IMPLEMENTED TOO MANY FEATURES ALREADY! You will never release this update if you keep indulging yourself! Stop it!â.

It has been revealed that lane markings made the scale of a scene easier to read. Naturally, that led me to the ultimate human-scale feature: humans! But I couldnât just throw the first set of free human models I found on the internet into the package. I did a fairly extensive search for a suitable pre-made model with both male and female variants, but to no avail. I had some requirements:.

Sources indicate that I couldnât find a model that met these requirements with a suitable redistribution license. So I decided this was a great opportunity to learning something upcoming: mesh sculpting in VR! I pulled out my Quest 3 and downloaded Shapelabs, which after a bit of practice and futzing around got me exactly what I wanted. Low-poly, but still human enough that you can read the pose at a glance.

From Shapelabs, the models went into Blender as GLB files for rigging and posing, then out as compact OBJ meshes for the package:.

In a recent development, compressed, theyâre roughly 18â21 KB each, checking the filesize box. Both model variants stand about 6 feet tall, with consistent proportions across their poses. Finally, a unit of measurement you can relate to!

According to recent reports, the original plot_gg() was based on a simple idea: take a ggplot2 object, turn a fill or color aesthetic into height, and map the original plot onto that extruded surface. This made it possible to create 3D ggplots without learning a separate 3D plotting API. Just drop in your existing plot and poof! A 3D version would appear.

But this came with one limitation: the data had to be attached to the surface.

Recent findings suggest that floating data needs something to ground it. I originally kept the data attached to the surface deliberately: actual 3D data is harder to understand on a 2D screen, since depth is ambiguous. Extruded 2D surfaces provide a continuous underlying substrate, which makes interpretation easierâthe surface itself provides depth cues, by nature of surface continuity providing cues on depth ordering. Itâs not hard to plop down some floating 3D data in a box and call it a day: before rayshader, that was what pretty much every 3D plotting library I encountered did. In my opinion, that lazy approach helped give 3D dataviz its terrible reputation. Adding 3D data disconnected from that substrate requires additional care and thought to keep the data interpretable.

In rayshader 1.0, plot_gg() is much more tightly integrated with the render_*() family of functions that add real 3D data to the scene. Rayshader now extracts the data extent from the existing ggplot2 scene. Basically, we now track how ggplot2 transforms data into the image, so we can use the same transformation for our 3D data. Downstream render calls can use that extent to place real 3D geometry in the correct part of the plot. The ggplot is no longer just a surface extrusion: itâs now the base coordinate system for a complete 3D scene.

It has been revealed that and this can really help visually, as that surface extrusion wasnât ideal for certain types of data. The original raster extrusion worked well for smooth surfaces, density plots, and continuous fields, but sharp polygon boundaries and abrupt vertical edges were harder.

According to recent reports, take Figure 19: it shows a map of US states with height mapped to population. States share an boundary in the source polygons, but when rasterized to row of pixels, you can see the colors bleed down the step between states. This is an unavoidable problem when you try to force vector data into a raster format. So we avoid it by drawing the actual 3D data. On the right, each stateâs own polygon makes a crisp vertical wall.

The same integration lets individual points float above a flat ggplot2 substrate (enabled with plot_gg(..., flat_substrate = TRUE)). The ggplot establishes the scales and coordinate system, and rayshader adds the observed values as actual 3D points, positioned correctly. render_zaxis() gives those floating marks a scale you can read. It picks up the height scale from the ggplot, and you can put the axis inside a panel or along the outer edge of the plot. If you have facets, you can pick the panel. It works on regular terrain maps, too.

This removes a ton of visual compromises. Instead of forcing every feature to become part of the surface texture, we use the surface texture as the base and add the features as real 3D geometry. The plot layout and elements are still determined by ggplot2: weâre just adding data to the z-axis.

It has been revealed that faceted plots can receive geometry one panel at a time. Spatial plots built with coord_sf() carry their geographic transform into the scene, too. Your base plot can use familiar geomsâgeom_hex(), geom_point(), geom_path(), geom_raster(), or geom_sf()âwhile rayshader adds polygons, points, paths, and a labeled z-axis in those coordinates.

Recent findings suggest that 3D ggplots were always a cool, sometimes useful novelty. Now they can be a foundation for complex 3D visualizations. How complex are we talking about? Watch me demo it below with a data visualization showing ADSB flight path data over Washington, DC. Come fly over the National Mall with me and Iâll walk you through how deep the 3D rabbit hole goes.

The render_*() functions have been rewritten around the same principle: spatial data already encodes where it is, so there is no reason to throw that information out.

In a recent development, render_points() can accept spatial point objects. render_path() can accept spatial line objects. render_label() can accept points, multipoints, polygons, and multipolygons, converting polygon inputs to centroids when needed. render_polygons() and render_beveled_polygons() use cached heightmap and extent metadata. render_buildings() uses spatial footprints, roof materials, roof angles, height columns, and CRS-aware extent filtering. render_obj() can place OBJ models using spatial point data. You can see most of these in action in Figure 22.

Industry observers note that thereâs some latest basic hillshading options as well. haze_shade() adds an RGBA haze overlay based on an exponential atmospheric model. It is useful for low-elevation haze, valley haze, and scenes where you want the atmosphere to participate in the map rather than sit behind it. It is a good way to subtly separate mountain tops from valleys.

In a recent development, radiance_shade() renders a top-down radiance pass from a cached hillshade context, the active 3D scene, or a supplied heightmap. It gives 2D maps and 3D ggplot2 workflows access to more visually-striking physically based lighting without forcing the entire project into a final path-traced render. This is a nice way to get higher-quality shadows on a model you can still rotate and revise quickly. The result is still an RGBA overlay, so it can be composited back into the usual rayshader map pipeline or exported to other programs.

Sources indicate that for a small area, we can usually ignore Earthâs curvature. As a map grows to cover hundreds or thousands of kilometers, the bend of the Earth can become an important part of the story. For satellite orbits, long-distance flight paths, and regional coverage maps, curvature can help signal to the reader that weâre dealing with global-scale data without an explicit scale bar.

Setting earth_curvature = TRUE in plot_3d() adds that curvature to the scene. Mountains and valleys can look flatter beside the much larger bend of the Earth when no vertical exaggeration is applied, but the adjustment gives those other GIS layers a more useful spatial context.

In a recent development, for example, Figure 25 demonstrates three Starlink satellites cross Alaska along paths calculated from real orbital data. Their simulated beams track populated places below, switching targets as they move within reach. Both views show the same moment, but on the right, the surface and orbital altitudes are adjusted to match the global curvature. This helps give the viewer key context clues for the spatial scales weâre dealing with here that the flat projection does not provide.

It has been revealed that want to realistically light a scene at a very specific time and date? Just give rayshader a date and timeâit already knows the place. For a scene with cached spatial coordinates, render_highquality(datetime = ...) can infer the location and generate the corresponding sky and sunlight. You donât need to look up the latitude, longitude, or sun angle again. Depending on the sky model, that can include stars, planets, and the moonâs phase and brightness.

According to recent reports, as an example, around the equinoxes, the low sun lines up with the National Mallâs eastâwest axisâa favorite alignment for photographers. On March 25, 2026, at 6:56:11 p.m. EDT, the modeled shadow of the Washington Monument runs parallel to the Mallâs main paths. A few days past the equinox, the sun is still high enough at that alignment to keep the shadow within this view.

And separately, text and annotation lines were physical objects in the rendered scene. Their letters and lines cast shadows across the terrain and buildings, giving annotations the same simulated weight as the things they were annotating. A label should help you read the map without becoming another object in it.

The labels in Figure 27 are drawn in screen space: their positions stay attached to the map, while the text keeps its size and faces the camera throughout the orbit, without casting shadows over the volcanoes. The horsepower axis in Figure 20 uses the same approach. The lines and text are composited in real time when youâre looking at the high quality preview render in rayrender, so you can set up the shot exactly how you want to. Oh, and you can set deferred_render = TRUE now as well, which removes the sample timer so you can have all the time in the world to set up your render. This is especially important now, since rayrender is now fully GPU-accellerated on ARM macs, leading to 30-50x speedups in rendering performance, so your render can often end before you got a chance to click on the screen. This blog post, however, is about rayshader, so I wonât steal its thunder talking about the awesome improvements in rayrender :).

Itâs been a long, properly textured roadâwhy 1.0 after eight years? I now feel that rayshader has firmly found its niche and purpose, and this overhaul feels like a graduation moment for the package. Iâm no longer figuring out what a 3D GIS workflow in R should feel likeâitâs now about making that workflow work for you. And thinking about all the people who used rayshader to produce everything from beautiful generative art and frameable cartographic works to scientific articles and award winning journalism made me decide to give rayshader the graduation it deserves, and make sure it knows: Youâre number 1.0!

Rayshader wouldnât be possible without the work of all the packages and people that supported it and provided great user feedback during its development. In a normal blog post, this is where normally youâd have a list of citations and people to thank. But how often does Râs most cinematic package get a 1.0 release? I decided the people, packages, and data behind rayshader deserved the full cinematic treatment that rayshader has provided the R ecosystem. And that the cinematic treatment should be created entirely in R, using rayrender, of course. Please stick around and hit play for the credits belowâand be sure to turn the sound on.
