#154274. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4739 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • It has been revealed that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Recent findings suggest that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

It has been revealed that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

Recent findings suggest that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash newly introduced competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

In a recent development, I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

Industry observers note that RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

In a recent development, recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The organization’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

According to recent reports, but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

Industry observers note that introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Recent findings suggest that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Recent findings suggest that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

According to recent reports, A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

In a recent development, last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky rapidly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a recent development, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

It has been revealed that though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the firm’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Recent findings suggest that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted intends for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the organization judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Industry observers note that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

According to recent reports, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.
  • The Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium.
  • In a recent development, about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.

The Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium. Work had carried on for months at the site in Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles without a valid permit. The order came on Thursday, days after Greenpeace Belgium asked the regional government to step in.

In a recent development, about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT. The Walloon infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, had revealed an investigation on Wednesday.

Sources indicate that google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centres cooled by air. In 2025 the company changed its aims. It merged two of the buildings into one larger building and switched to cooling with water from the Sambre river, Greenpeace remarked.

Industry observers note that the Walloon administration approved that amended permit in April 2026. After residents appealed, Desquesnes revoked it in August. The request covered 600 cubic metres of river water an hour, the minister said. Less than a quarter of it would have gone back into the river, according to Belga.

Recent findings suggest that residents then told Greenpeace that work was still going on. The group investigated, using satellite images, and launched an emergency procedure earlier this week.

Recent findings suggest that “Tech giants are not above the law,” noted Nadia Cornejo, a Greenpeace Belgium spokesperson. “This should already have been the case in August, when the permit was cancelled.”.

Google appealed the revocation but did not wait for the court to rule before carrying on with the work, VRT reported.

Google is committed to “an open and collaborative dialogue with the regional government and experts” on its investments in Wallonia, a spokesperson told VRT.

On 17 October it asked Belgium’s Council of State to annul and suspend the minister’s decision. Greenpeace and several residents asked to join the case on 16 November, and a public hearing is set for 7 January.

In a recent development, data centres have faced similar local opposition elsewhere. Google’s Finnish data centre project drew a police investigation, and residents in Indonesia’s Batam protested over water in October. In the US, voters rejected data centre measures at the midterms.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called it a “serious cyber incident”, and Downing Street said there is right now no evidence of customer data loss.
  • Recent findings suggest that the UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident.
  • “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department stated in its statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called it a “serious cyber incident”, and Downing Street said there is right now no evidence of customer data loss. Some claimants told the BBC their payments had not arrived. TNW has updated this article.

Recent findings suggest that the UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident. The department, which runs Universal Credit, the state pension and most other British benefits, confirmed the incident on Friday morning.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department stated in its statement.

In a recent development, the department says the incident does not affect regular benefit and pension payments, which will arrive as normal. People who need help can call their usual benefit line.

It has been revealed that the systems for pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment applications are down, the BBC reported. So are Tell Us Once, which people use to report a death, and state pension applications.

Sources indicate that mcFadden stated the department was aware of an problem on Thursday and “did the right thing” by taking services down to protect people’s personal details. He said there was no evidence that the incident had compromised anyone’s data.

“When we get an incident like this, the most vital thing to do is to protect the public,” McFadden mentioned, according to the BBC.

Industry observers note that the Prime Minister’s official spokesperson called it a “live and ongoing incident”. Officials could not rule out that a malicious actor was behind it.

Industry observers note that “Presently there is no evidence of customer data loss. But the investigation is ongoing so I’m not going to get ahead of that process,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added there was no evidence that a malicious actor had targeted other government departments. DWP is working with the National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre.

Some Universal Credit claimants told the BBC they had not received their payments on Friday. DWP stated the incident had not affected regular payments. It asked anyone with problems to call its benefit phone line.

According to recent reports, debbie Abrahams, who chairs the Work and Pensions Committee, said taking systems offline was “absolutely the right thing”. Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science and Technology Committee, said the disruption “should be a wake up call”.

“Quite often we are working on extremely old computer systems,” DWP’s permanent secretary, Sarah Healey, told MPs on 4 November.

In 2025-26, DWP spent £309.5bn on benefits and pensions for about 23 million people, its annual report indicates.

Attacks in 2025 disrupted Jaguar Land Rover, Marks & Spencer and other British firms. Last year, the UK’s privacy regulator also fined outsourcing firm Capita £14m over a 2023 breach that exposed pension scheme data, after initially planning a £45m penalty.

In a recent development, DWP is the second major institution in two days to take systems offline over a cyber incident. News agency AFP took its content platform offline on Thursday. In the US, a FinCEN hack took Treasury systems offline this week, and Switzerland reported AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, US sanctions pushed Huawei and China into self-reliance, and Huawei’s founder, Ren Zhengfei, wants Donald Trump thanked for it.
  • “Pass on our thanks to him, and also share the story of the Trump Corridor as well,” Ren told the Times.
  • It has been revealed that huawei executives call a gilded hallway at the headquarters the Trump Corridor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, US sanctions pushed Huawei and China into self-reliance, and Huawei’s founder, Ren Zhengfei, wants Donald Trump thanked for it. Ren spoke to Keith Bradsher and Adam Satariano of The New York Times at Huawei’s Shenzhen headquarters in October. The paper published the interview on Thursday.

“Pass on our thanks to him, and also share the story of the Trump Corridor as well,” Ren told the Times.

It has been revealed that huawei executives call a gilded hallway at the headquarters the Trump Corridor. It is named after the president whose first-term campaign tried to cut Huawei off from advanced chips and global telecoms networks. After the crackdown, Ren said, Huawei became “a organization of our own country”. He is 82 and still Huawei’s chief executive.

Recent findings suggest that the interview ran two days after a federal jury in New York convicted Huawei. The jury found it guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets from US companies and of bank fraud linked to Iran. Huawei said the verdicts were “without legal or factual merit”.

Industry observers note that it also came as the US tightened its curbs on Nvidia’s chips. On 16 November the US moved to restrict remote access to American AI chips through overseas data centres. Huawei’s Ascend processors have become China’s leading alternative to Nvidia’s chips, the Times reported.

Huawei now spends more than $27bn a year on research and development, according to the Times. It has worked with Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, to adapt their models to its chips. It argues it can rival Nvidia by linking many processors into one large system, even if each chip is weaker.

In a recent development, the gap remains wide. Huawei will make less than 4% as much AI computing power as Nvidia this year, research firm Epoch AI estimates. Its most powerful chip, the Ascend 950, delivers about half the performance of Nvidia’s H100, which began shipping in 2022.

China also still lacks the most advanced chipmaking equipment, including lithography machines from the Dutch firm ASML. Huawei has been working to fill other gaps at home, including its own AI memory.

Many in Trump’s first administration believed the restrictions could destroy Huawei, the Times reported.

“We thought this could be a death blow,” Liza Tobin, then a China policy official at the National Security Council, told the Times.

Sources indicate that ren, speaking before Nvidia’s recent leadership turmoil, mentioned China would eventually overtake the US in chips. “It’s just a matter of time,” he said. He said he still hoped the two countries could repair their relationship.

“We have now established a complete chain that allows us to survive,” Ren told the Times.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It has been revealed that it’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app. These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

More significant to me personally, the revision also seems to have fixed a longstanding CarPlay bug regarding playlist sorting.

Industry observers note that I use custom sorting for several of my playlists in Apple Music, and before iOS 27.2, my sort settings didn’t carry over from iPhone to CarPlay. Fortunately that’s now been fixed, as Reddit customers have reported too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that whether you're ready to dive headfirst into the Christmas spirit or craving something heavier, this weekend's lineup has you covered. We've got a cozy, second-chance holiday rom-com adapted from a beloved Jill Shalvis novel, an intimate Spanish drama starring Belén Cuesta and Karra Elejalde about a community coping with a devastating 1980s tragedy, and a moody, Vincent Cassel-led French period piece that reimagines the legend of Quasimodo amid the turmoil of 1830s Paris.

That should keep you busy through the umpteenth helping of leftover stuffing, yeah? Here are three fresh-to-Netflix movies to add to your weekend watchlist.

Sure, we've got a few more days until December arrives, but if you want to get into the holiday spirit early, a yuletide rom-com is an easy entry point. Based on the second of the Heartbreaker Bay novels by Jill Shalvis, this Christmastime romance centers on San Francisco pet shop owner Willa Davis (Rachel Melvin), who, a decade after Keane Winters (Thomas Beaudoin) stood her up in high school, re-encounters the fella who slighted her when he comes into her shop in need of a cat sitter for the holidays.

Recent findings suggest that though Willa still harbors a grudge, she unexpectedly falls for Keane — even though he doesn't remember hurting her all those years ago. Directed by Ashley Avis, the 2017 film also stars Flo Lawrence, Alexandra Weaver, and Annie Thurman.

Watch "The Trouble with Mistletoe" on Netflix now.

Inspired by a real-world tragedy — the October 1980 gas explosion at the Marcelino Ugalde public school in Ortuella, Spain — this Spanish drama stars Belén Cuesta and Karra Elejalde as Mariaje and Nicasio, respectively, a mother and grandfather whose lives are irreversibly changed after losing nine-year-old Nuco (Alex Infantes) in a gas explosion at his school.

Based on the novel of the same name by Fernando Aramburu and adapted by writer-director Mariano Barroso, "The Child" weaves a fictional story around the real-life tragedy, showing how not only individuals have to grapple with their personal grief and loss but also Whole communities and, in the case of Spain, entire countries.

Watch "The Child" on Netflix now.

You already know Victor Hugo's "The Hunchback of Notre-Dame," but while that classic French tale is famously set in 15th-century Paris, this Netflix adaptation moves up the action to 1830 on the eve of the July Revolution, around when Hugo himself published his most famous work.

As political turmoil and cholera threaten to ravage the City of Light, a hunchbacked stonemason named Quasimodo (played by César winner Vincent Cassel), believed to resist the disease, is hunted down by police for medical experiments. Things get even more complicated when Quasimodo falls for a dancer named Agnès (Daphné Patakia), an unrequited love that leads the hunchback to risk everything to keep her safe.

Watch "The Hunchback, Soul of Paris" on Netflix now.

For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

It has been revealed that enterprise software and cloud infrastructure organization Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

Industry observers note that after hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

Recent findings suggest that "We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

In a recent development, while Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as fresh contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," noted Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space tech giant with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

According to recent reports, gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst noted, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

Recent findings suggest that gesuale ranks No. 369 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17%. See Rocket Lab Statistics on TipRanks.

It has been revealed that J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth recently upgraded Meta Platforms (META) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $820 from $640. Despite the year-to-date underperformance of META, the 5-star analyst still sees significant upside, as Meta is in the early stages of launching frontier models and AI-powered offerings beyond advertising, particularly the Muse AI agent and Meta Model API access.

"Frontier models are at the core of Meta's product and monetization pipeline over a multi-year period, and its path toward superintelligence," stated Anmuth.

In the summer of 2025, Meta set a goal to rebuild its Meta Superintelligence Labs team and deliver frontier AI models within a year, the analyst said. The team appears to have met its goal, rapidly advancing from the rollout of Muse Spark 1.1 in July to Muse Spark 1.3, which is competitive with Claude and GPT models, Anmuth said.

Meanwhile, Meta's Watermelon product will expand opportunities in consumer products, business intelligence, and Family of Apps engagement, the analyst said. The product will enhance internal operations and overall efficiency, said Anmuth, who's confident of Meta's ability to bring consumer-driven AI products to its extensive user base of 4 billion and views its distribution network as a competitive advantage.

While Meta has focused on frontier models and AI product development, Anmuth also sees solid opportunity in its AI infrastructure capacity, which he believes will support future compute needs.

Anmuth ranks No. 832 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of about 9.40%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring latest challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also indicates how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

Shoppers ask AI for Black Friday deals, but few let the bots pay

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, traffic from AI services to US retail sites more than doubled on Thanksgiving from last year, Adobe told the Associated Press.
  • Recent findings suggest that purchases made by AI agents are a far smaller slice.
  • It has been revealed that this weekend is the biggest test yet for the shopping agents from Meta, Google, OpenAI and Amazon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, traffic from AI services to US retail sites more than doubled on Thanksgiving from last year, Adobe told the Associated Press. Shoppers spent a record $7.1bn online that day, up 10.4%. Adobe expects $12.9bn on Black Friday itself.

Recent findings suggest that purchases made by AI agents are a far smaller slice. They made up 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of their value, according to Bain & Co research. Annie Palmer reported the figures for CNBC.

It has been revealed that this weekend is the biggest test yet for the shopping agents from Meta, Google, OpenAI and Amazon. Each wants to help people find gifts and, in time, buy them. The early evidence points to three problems. Shoppers do not trust the bots with their money. Many retailers will not let them in. And nobody agrees who pays when an agent gets it wrong.

Industry observers note that A Morning Consult poll for Visa found that 54% of adults have used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year. Only 23% trust generative AI to make payments for them, Phil Wahba reported for Fortune.

The price of the item matters too. In an American Express survey, 52% of US consumers were happy for an agent to buy cheap items such as groceries. Only 15% felt the same about electronics and appliances, the substantial sellers of Black Friday.

It has been revealed that that caution has some basis. Visa sent 22 AI models on 15 shopping tasks earlier this month, and they failed 42.8% of their runs. In more than half of the failed runs, the agent still bought something.

In a recent development, british shoppers are trying the tools too. Meta launched Muse in the UK this week, with partners including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys. A third of people planning to shop in the sales intend to use AI, up from 19% last year, according to a YouGov poll. Almost half of the shoppers who use AI worry about biased or sponsored results, Sarah Butler reported in The Guardian.

It has been revealed that even shoppers who want an agent to buy for them may find it cannot. About half of big retailers and popular brands do not let AI assistants shop their sites. London software firm Human Forward found this after testing ChatGPT, Gemini, Muse and other agents on 200 websites, Spencer Soper reported for Bloomberg.

According to recent reports, amazon has gone furthest. It blocked Muse from its store in September. It is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser, in a case due for trial next year. Amazon is reportedly in talks with Meta about Muse, but the block is still in place.

“Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience,” an Amazon spokesperson told Bloomberg.

Amazon’s advertising business is expected to bring in $81.9bn this year, Bloomberg reported. Bots that browse for shoppers could undercut it. Chief executive Andy Jassy told investors in October that outside agents were not meaningfully hurting its ads business.

“The natural question is whether agentic shopping from external horizontal agents is meaningfully impacting Amazon ads, and the answer is no,” Jassy stated on Amazon’s earnings call.

Other companies limit agents rather than ban them. eBay, United Airlines and Kohl’s restrict what agents can do or block them, CNBC reported. Some retailers let bots browse but stop them at the checkout. Agents that do get in can still get stuck at logins and CAPTCHA tests.

In a recent development, maia Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, told CNBC she asked Muse to buy windscreen wipers from AutoZone. Seventeen hours later, the agent stated AutoZone had cancelled the order over an error. Its suggestion was to buy them on Amazon herself.

It has been revealed that the bigger question for retailers is liability. Some have written their answer into their terms of service. Best Buy treats an agent’s purchases as if the customer had made them.

“Best Buy is not responsible for conduct, errors, actions, or inaction by any Digital Agent,” the company’s terms state.

Card and payment companies are taking on some of that risk. American Express has noted it will protect eligible customers from charges caused by an agent’s errors. Stripe, whose Link wallet works with Muse, offers a refund guarantee on some agent purchases. JPMorgan Chase went the other way last month and blocked outside agents from acting for its customers, citing security, CNBC reported.

According to recent reports, in the UK, TrueLayer is testing another route. Its pilot lets an agent pay by bank at Papa John’s, under the FCA’s watch.

“In Europe especially, retailers are asking a simple question: if the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?” Mark Howell, director of European retail at e-commerce firm Rithum, told The Guardian.

Meta says that in the UK, Muse must ask for approval before it buys anything. A separate “security agent” checks its actions against the permissions a user has granted.

Sources indicate that the tech companies are pressing on. Muse reached 10 million users in the US and Canada about six weeks after its September launch, Bloomberg reported. Mark Zuckerberg told investors in October that shopping was its most common use, with users spending $200 on average. He expects Meta to take a small fee from transactions. Google has introduced Universal Cart, which puts items from several retailers in one basket.

McKinsey estimates agentic commerce could generate $1tn of US economic activity by 2030. Retailers, meanwhile, are bracing for more AI-driven cyberattacks around the sales.

Matt Kochmann, a tech executive, tried ChatGPT, Muse and Claude to find a case for his new iPhone. None of them stood out, he told Bloomberg.

“It just doesn’t feel magical yet,” he remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been just over a year since Apple released AirPods Pro 3, and I can confidently say I’ve worn them every day since. After a year of heavy use, I’m even more convinced that AirPods Pro 3 are the best money you can spend on Apple gear (especially at current sale pricing).

According to recent reports, while the changes to AirPods Pro 3 fit have been controversial to some customers, I’ve been thoroughly impressed over the last year. I find them incredibly comfortable, and I absolutely notice the improvement in noise cancellation enabled by the updated in-ear fit. The sound quality, of course, is also excellent, and is made better by the updated shape.

It has been revealed that one feature I haven’t found myself using (or noticing) very often is the heart rate sensor. This is probably because I always wear an Apple Watch. Apple claims that AirPods Pro 3 and Apple Watch can work together to get you the most accurate heart rate data possible. I assume this happens in the background, but I never notice or think about it.

An interesting twist to AirPods Pro 3 is that they actually have worse battery life on paper than AirPods Pro 2.

In a recent development, I haven’t noticed the overall lower battery life at all. On long travel days, however, I absolutely appreciate the longer battery life from the buds themselves. I can now comfortably wear them from my departure airport to my arrival airport on most travel days. And I don’t have any problems just placing my AirPods Pro 3 on a Qi charger on my desk to refuel.

One thing I love about AirPods is that they continuously get better with software updates. AirPods Pro 3 are no different. In addition to bug fixes and performance improvements, here are some of the new features that have come to AirPods Pro 2 since they were released:.

Here’s what I wrote in my AirPods Pro 3 review last year:.

According to recent reports, I often tell people that AirPods are the best bang-for-your-buck product in Apple’s lineup. They’re one of my most-used Apple products, and I’m sure I could do some math to prove they have the lowest cost-per-use of anything I own. AirPods Pro 3 are the best $249 you can spend with Apple today, and they feel like a turning point in what we should expect from the category going forward.

One year later, I stand by this paragraph. Also, note that I wrote $249 in that paragraph. Right now, AirPods Pro 3 are on sale for $149. That is an absolutely absurd value. If you’re on the fence, there’s never been a better time to join the AirPods Pro 3 club.

The significant day (Nov 27) has arrived and the Black Friday deals are rolling in on headphones from all of the major brands, including Apple, Bose, Sony and more.

Industry observers note that I'm Pete, senior reviews editor here at Tom's Guide, and this is my fifth Black Friday covering deals. This year, I've been keeping close tabs on the best headphones deals.

Most impressive for me are the deals we're seeing on flagships. The Apple AirPods Max 2 from are reduced from $549 to $419 at Amazon. That's $130 off this year's model! Likewise, the Sony WH-1000XM6 have seen a hefty discount, dropping from $459 to $348 at Amazon.

Those are just the significant names though, and there are lots more deals to be had. If you're looking to upgrade your sound this Black Friday, all you need to do is read on.

Soundcore's Q20i have dropped in price for Black Friday. They're comfortable, lightweight and sound great for the price, while also offering ANC. Seriously, for under 40 bucks, you can't complain.

Recent findings suggest that in our Sony WH-CH530 review, we gave these plucky little cans a full five stars. Why? Because look at that $69 MSRP. That's why. For the money, these cans offer stellar sound, plenty of comfort, solid battery life and fun colorways! And now they're just $38.

Sources indicate that the Skullcandy Crusher Evo literally have a bass slider in them to make your head wobble! So if it's bass you're after, and you fancy $120 off, this one's for you.

According to recent reports, there was only one thing we didn't like in our Sony WH-CH730N review, and that was the U.S. MSRP of $199. Well, that's changed with this deal. For $99, the WH-CH730N are a hell of a lot of headphones for the money.

Great fit, finish, sound and noise cancelling — the JBL Live 780NC are some impressive mid-range cans. And this Black Friday deal makes them even better.

The venerable Beats Studio Pro. but this time... $200 off MSRP! Solid ANC? Check. A cool, stylish look? Check. Good sound quality? This isn't a deal to pass up.

Bose might have replaced the QuietComfort headphones with a newer (also reduced) pair, but at this price, the OG QuietComforts are still a super tempting deal. Excellent ANC, a comfortable fit, and increasingly-rare-these-days physical controls.

The Nothing Headphone (1) certainly look the part, and can help you live out your Cyberpunk dreams while offering solid customizable sound and a great control scheme.

In a recent development, these may have been succeeded by the Momentum 5, but that doesn't make them any less impressive, especially given this massive $120 saving. The Sennheiser Momentum 4 are seriously good value at this price.

Sony recently relaunched the original XM4, hence the XM4C. These updated cans now have Bluetooth 6.0, a new removable and replaceable battery, and some AI audio upscaling. The XM4 were still fantastic anyway — even in 2026. But new features is never a bad thing, and nor is $101 off.

According to recent reports, remember earlier when I stated Bose had replaced the original QuietComforts? Well, the fresh ones are right here and also on sale at $160 off! If you want some snazzier colors but similarly powerful ANC and that warm Bose sound, you've found the cans for you — the Bose QuietComfort Headphones 2nd gen.

These Sonos cans earned an impressive 4.5 stars in our Sonos Ace review. The sound and noise cancelling were on point, as was the battery life, the design and the integration with other Sonos gear. And now they're $120 off!

According to recent reports, the Beats 360 are the latest in the Beats range (seriously, they only launched like 2 months ago) and ideal for working out. Sony's XM6 are the latest flagships. They weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. Flagship quality, and now mid-range price.

  • In a recent development, chinese EV maker Xpeng will start mass-producing its Iron humanoid robot in January, the firm said at its AI Day this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xpeng’s robots over the years, with the latest Iron humanoid on the far right.

Chinese EV maker Xpeng will start mass-producing its Iron humanoid robot in January 2027 and train it as a store assistant first. Its co-president Brian Gu says it could reach homes in one or two years, priced like one of Xpeng’s cars, with tens of thousands of sales targeted next year.

In a recent development, chinese EV maker Xpeng will start mass-producing its Iron humanoid robot in January, the firm said at its AI Day this week. Co-president Brian Gu told CNBC it could be doing household chores in “one or two years”.

Recent findings suggest that first, Iron will train as a store assistant in Xpeng’s shops from early 2027. Gu noted the firm could then “start thinking about deploying into home settings”.

The robot has 76 degrees of freedom, the separate ways its body can move, and more than 1,500 touch sensors. It runs on three of Xpeng’s own Turing AI chips, the same family it puts in its cars. Xpeng’s latest production line is designed to finish one every 2.5 minutes at full speed.

Gu told Bloomberg TV that Xpeng aims to sell “tens of thousands” of Iron robots in 2027, with public sales from the second quarter. He expects it to cost about as much as one of Xpeng’s cars, which sell for 119,800 yuan (about $18,000) to 309,800 yuan.

“It’s much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business,” Gu told CNBC.

Industry observers note that xpeng’s robotics unit raised more than $900M in August ahead of the production run. Rival carmaker BYD has also been readying a humanoid for its showrooms.

Xpeng is one of many Chinese firms racing to scale up. Morgan Stanley expects China to ship 50,000 humanoids this year, and Chinese firms already build almost every humanoid sold worldwide.

You also get a reliable kill switch, multi-hop connections, IP rotation, which swaps your IP address every few seconds in six countries, and Mimic, Norton's own stealth protocol, which disguises your VPN traffic so it's harder to block on restrictive networks.

Two years ago when Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on Apple’s forthcoming HomeView, I was immediately ready to buy one.

According to recent reports, after numerous delays, the HomeView is finally here. And despite several shortcomings I expect will be fixed with software updates, the HomeView overall is exactly what I’ve been wanting in a home product.

HomeView is essentially a HomePod, but with a screen. And that screen adds so much extra value.

When rumors said the HomeView would only have a 7-inch display, I was concerned it would be too small. It turns out, Apple knew what it was doing. The HomeView’s size is a feature, not a bug. Too much larger and it would stand out as a piece of tech. By staying small, the HomeView can be a cute, non-distracting addition to the home.

Here are some HomeView features I’ve been loving so far:.

According to recent reports, none of these is what I’d call a “killer feature,” but together they amount to a delightful experience. I already liked having a HomePod around, and HomeView builds on that foundation in so many ways.

Overall, HomeView is very much the product I was hoping for back in 2024. That remarked, there’s definitely room for improvement. Here’s what’s missing.

Sources indicate that I love HomeView for what it is today, but I fully expect Apple to improve the product via software updates. Leaks already point to two major feature upgrades in the works that I hope ship soon.

Sources indicate that built-in apps for Apple Photos and Notes would be great to have, plus support for the recipes included in Apple News+. But my personal top request is for parental controls of some sort.

Recent findings suggest that really? One of the very few people who will purchase this product.

What exactly are you planning to use Homeview for, that your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, can't already do for you?

Industry observers note that for a device that’s intended for the whole family, I’ve been surprised to find there are no current features to prevent young children from doing whatever they want with HomeView. I have a toddler who loves the HomeView so much that I had to move it out of his reach. I wish there was a way to lock the screen on command, or prevent switching apps or faces without authentication. Some sort of “toddler mode” would be greatly appreciated.

Siri AI has also had some bugs, but those are likely related to me running the iOS 27.3 beta.

Apple’s fresh HomeView is available now for $299.

Electric cars beat petrol and diesel combined in the EU by almost 70,000

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (350 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the EU registered 279,799 battery-electric cars in October, up 61.4%, while petrol and diesel sales each fell about 30%, leaving EVs almost 70,000 ahead of the two combined, ACEA data highlights.
  • Electric cars outsold petrol and diesel cars combined in the EU in October, InsideEVs reported, based on figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).
  • The EU registered 279,799 battery-electric cars last month, up 61.4% from a year earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the EU registered 279,799 battery-electric cars in October, up 61.4%, while petrol and diesel sales each fell about 30%, leaving EVs almost 70,000 ahead of the two combined, ACEA data highlights. Hybrids still lead the market, and combustion cars remain ahead for the year so far.

Electric cars outsold petrol and diesel cars combined in the EU in October, InsideEVs reported, based on figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).

The EU registered 279,799 battery-electric cars last month, up 61.4% from a year earlier. Petrol sales fell 30% to 158,970 and diesel sales fell 31% to 51,177. That left EVs almost 70,000 cars ahead of the two combined.

A year earlier, petrol and diesel cars outsold EVs by about 127,000, InsideEVs calculated. Electric cars took 29.8% of the EU market in October, while total registrations rose 2.6% to 939,447. A growing range of cheaper models is giving buyers more reasons to switch.

According to recent reports, germany and France drove much of the jump. Germany registered 94,086 EVs, up 60.7%, and France 61,958, up 79.4%. In June, EVs outsold every other fuel in Germany for the first time.

According to recent reports, chinese and US brands gained too. BYD registered 30,974 cars in the EU in October, up 128%, as Chinese carmakers push into Europe. Tesla’s registrations rose 83.5% to 10,166.

Sources indicate that hybrids are still the EU’s best-sellers. Full and mild hybrids took 36% of registrations from January to October, against 23.4% for battery-electric cars. Their popularity helps explain why Brussels has proposed softening its 2035 target so some can stay on sale.

According to recent reports, petrol and diesel cars also still lead for the year so far, with 2.61 million registrations to 2.21 million for EVs. A year ago, they outsold EVs by more than two to one. In August, electric cars took 29% of newly introduced registrations across Europe.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's no denying it: gaming hardware, accessories and video games are expensive.
  • Games are huge and require lots of space these days.
  • In a recent development, and then, the solution came to me in the form of a glorious PS5 internal SSD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's no denying it: gaming hardware, accessories and video games are expensive. But you know what softens the blow a bit? Grabbing a fantastic deal during Black Friday and saving big bucks. As a tech journalist and senior reviews writer, it's my job to bring the greatest deals to you — and I've found one for those short on console storage.

Games are huge and require lots of space these days. Take GTA 6 as an example. It came out a week ago and people scrambled to free up 210GB of space on their PS5 to make room for it — myself included. Now, I'm one of those people who hates deleting their favorite games just to make space for a new one. I scratched my head, asking myself, "Do I delete Cyberpunk? Or do I delete Assassin's Creed Shadows?".

In a recent development, and then, the solution came to me in the form of a glorious PS5 internal SSD. Enter the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 850P, which has just dropped in price especially for Black Friday. In both the U.S. and the U.K., you can save on the plug-and-play SSD.

In a recent development, if you're based in the U.K. like I am, both the 1TB and 2TB versions of the internal SSD are discounted. You can get the 1TB version for just £222 at Amazon, and the 2TB version for £545.

According to recent reports, the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 850P is available in four storage configurations: 1TB, 2TB, 4TB and 8TB. The 2TB version is currently discounted in the U.S., available for $569 directly from PlayStation, as is the 4TB version, which is down to $899 at Amazon U.S.

The 850P is officially licensed by PlayStation and comes in four configurations: 1TB, 2TB, 4TB and 8TB. I've been using the 2TB version and it offers more than enough space for small and large games alike. As its name suggests, the 850P is an internal SSD, and there's a dedicated slot for M.2 NVMe drivers under your PS5's hood, regardless of the model.

What I love about the 850P is just how easy it is to use. This is a plug-and-play hard drive. To install it, you need to turn over your PS5 and pop out the top panel. You'll see a silver plate which you can unscrew using a small star screwdriver. Once that's done, you need to remove another screw (and its spacer), slot in your 850P, and put the screw and spacer back in.

Now all that's left to do is reinsert everything you took out and pop the PS5's panel back into place. Et voilà! You're good to go. Fire up your PS5 and you'll be prompted to format the 850P before using it. This takes under two minutes, and after that, you can start installing games.

You'll then be able to see the 850P appear as "M.2 SSD Storage" on the PS5's home screen — if you've got the storage widget active, of course. If not, you can dive into system settings to see if it's working a-okay (which it most certainly will be).

Sources indicate that the 850P offers fast read and write speeds. You get sequential read speeds up to 7,300 MB/s, which means that game loading times are rapid. There's barely any waiting time! Write speeds up to 6,600 MB/s also mean that copying from disc to console is supremely fast. I couldn't believe how quickly I was able to install Detroit Become Human!

Sources indicate that lastly, the 850P features heatsink which ensures the SSD remains cool and doesn't overheat. There's so much to love about this nifty little device, and as a PS5 owner, it's saved me the headache of deleting games every time I buy a new one.

Right now, you can grab the 4TB model for just $899 at Amazon U.S., and the 2TB version for £406 at Amazon U.K. These Black Friday deals are too good to pass up on, and I recommend grabbing them as soon as you can!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%.
  • In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.
  • Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud organization CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Industry observers note that recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

Recent findings suggest that "CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," noted Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

It has been revealed that chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

According to recent reports, after a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

In a recent development, over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and upcoming markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell stated. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell remarked.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he mentioned.

In a recent development, devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the organization if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he mentioned. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

Industry observers note that "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#154246. Citroën Hydraulic System
