Citroën Hydraulic System

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Citroën's hydropneumatic* suspension, despite a reputation for complexity, complication and unreliability is actually very simple in operation and very reliable and furthermore, offers an unrivalled level of comfort coupled with excellent handling and grip.
  • Recent findings suggest that the system takes advantage of the fact that you can compress a gas but cannot compress a fluid.
  • In a recent development, the system provides a soft, comfortable, yet well-controlled ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Citroën's hydropneumatic* suspension, despite a reputation for complexity, complication and unreliability is actually very simple in operation and very reliable and furthermore, offers an unrivalled level of comfort coupled with excellent handling and grip.

Recent findings suggest that the system takes advantage of the fact that you can compress a gas but cannot compress a fluid. Thus gas acts as the springing medium while the hydraulic fluid does all the clever things such as providing damping and levelling. Unlike the hydrolastic system fitted to certain BMC and BLMC cars, the Citroën system relies on an engine-driven pump to pressurise the hydraulic system and it is this power source which enables self-levelling, variable ride height, assisted jacking and zero roll (in the Activa Xantia) and also allows for fully powered braking systems and power steering too.

In a recent development, the system provides a soft, comfortable, yet well-controlled ride. The nitrogen springing medium is approximately six times more flexible than a conventional steel system, so self-leveling is incorporated to allow the vehicle to cope with the extraordinary suppleness provided. In the early fifties, France was noted for particularly poor road quality and therefore the only way to maintain a relatively high speed in a vehicle was if it could easily absorb road irregularities. It was this need that also drove the development of the 2CV's interconnected suspension system.

According to recent reports, in the DS, the high pressure hydraulic system also operated the clutch and gear change. With the introduction of the XM came electronic control of the suspension system - called Hydractive and a refined version of this system was fitted to high specification Xantias and to later XMs. The Hydractive system allowed for variable damping and automatic switching between soft and firm modes which allowed an unparalleled combination of ride comfort and good handling.

Recent findings suggest that hydropneumatic suspension was first shown in 1954 when it was fitted to the rear of the 15CV H Traction Avant . This was a foretaste of the system that was fitted to the astonishing DS 19 of 1955. Variants of the suspension have been fitted subsequently to the GS of 1970, the SM of the same year, the CX , the BX , the XM, the Xantia most C5s and the C6. Other cars fitted with the system were the M 35 Wankel-engined prototype, the GZ Birotor , some variants of the H van and various Rolls Royce and Mercedes-Benz cars where it was used under licence.

For an excellent technical guide in Adobe Acrobat format covering all Citroën's hydraulic systems, click here and follow the link to Technical Guide.

Above the Hydractive 2 system fitted to high specification variants of the Xantia and XM.

The system switches from "soft" to "firm" modes according to a number of parameters programmed into the on board computer.

Sensors provide the necessary input to the computer to determine which mode is appropriate.

A central sphere on each axle is switched in and out of circuit to alter the amount of suspension travel and damping.

According to recent reports, below left the Xantia front suspension comprises MacPherson type struts with the Hydropneumatic suspension spheres mounted on top. Each sphere contains a diaphragm behind which a quantity of nitrogen is trapped. A height corrector is attached to the anti roll bar and when a load is placed in the car, the car body sinks. This movement is registered by the height corrector which opens a valve to admit hydraulic fluid under pressure to "lengthen" the hydraulic strut and thereby re-establish the correct ride height. A control inside the car allows the ride height to be varied by the driver thereby aiding wheel changes.

The SC-CAR or Activa system builds on Hydractive 2 by incorporating hydraulic jacks to counter body roll.

Hydractive 2 is also fitted to most XM models.

Below right the rear suspension of the Xantia comprises trailing arms connected to an anti roll bar with height corrector attached.

The rear spheres lie flat which permits an unobstructed boot floor with no suspension unit intrusions.

It has been revealed that the hydraulic system acquired a reputation for unreliability when it was prematurely released on the DS. There were problems with seals and the fluid originally used was intensely hygroscopic (it absorbed water) which caused oxydisation and early DS drivers frequently discovered their pride and joy resting on its haunches in a pool of fluid. The introduction of LHS improved matters but it was not until a mineral oil LHM or Liquide Hydraulique Minéral was introduced in the mid sixties that the system became thoroughly reliable.

According to recent reports, in the DS, the hydraulic system provided power for the clutch, gearchange and steering. Additional uses of this system included the fully powered self centring steering system (DIRAVI or Varipower) fitted to the SM and CX, levelling of the headlamps fitted to the SM and a number of design studies were undertaken to investigate hydraulic operation of windscreen wipers, an air dam brake and even the opening and closing of windows.

Prior to the advent of cheap electronics, a totally hydraulic anti lock braking system had been built, together with zero roll suspension.

Electronics provided a cheap, low weight solution for active suspension and anti lock brakes.

Recent findings suggest that anti dive suspension is incorporated The rear brakes take their fluid from the rear suspension which pulls the tail down under heavy braking. On all hydraulic Citroëns (with the exception of some early ID 19s), the balance between front to rear braking effort is modified by the respective loads placed on the front and rear suspension.

Top left - suspension in "soft" state; the solenoid valve (1) is energised, the slide valve opens allowing hydraulic fluid to flow between the between the suspension cylinders and the spheres (4 and 3) via the dampers (6). All six spheres are in use.

Bottom left - suspension is in "firm" mode; the solenoid valve (1) is not energised, the slide valve takes up a position which blocks the movement of hydraulic fluid between the two main spheres (4) on each axle and isolates the additional spheres (3) from them both.

Above - a normally suspended car undertaking the slalom test.

High pressure hydraulics are the jewel in Citroën's crown. The hydropneumatic suspension system offers an unparalleled level of comfort and control although it must be admitted that it is not perfect. Cars without the Hydractive or Activa systems suffer from considerable body roll (the basic system is poor in roll stiffness); the ride tends to be slightly harsh at low speeds; the hydraulic system is very good at transmitting road noise into the cabin; some people suffer from motion sickness in an hydropneumatic Citroën; there is a tendency for pitching if one is heavy footed when driving a Citroën and some drivers dislike the feeling of being divorced from the road surface. The system can be caught out by hump backed bridges - the body rises from the road surface as the apex of the bridge is reached, the height corrector then decides the car body is raised too high and reduces ride height as the vehicle descends the other side of the bridge - the body then crashes into the suspension bump stops.

On the plus side, one can drive far quicker on indifferent road surfaces than might be believed possible (this goes a long way to explaining the success of the marque in motorsport) and handling is almost unaffected by a change in ride height caused by a full load.

Additional benefits include an absence of diagonal pitching, the constant ride height ensures headlamp beams are always properly aligned, irrespective of load and aerodynamics remain unaffected by load thanks to a constant angle of attack.

More prosaic but nevertheless useful benefits include the ability to drive on terrain that is normally restricted to off-road vehicles, the ability to raise or lower the suspension to assist in loading or unloading the vehicle, to assist in changing a wheel, to facilitate towing and to make washing of the car easier.

Above - the Xantia Activa undertaking the same slalom test at the same speed - note the total absence of body roll.

The C5 features a decentralised system employing separate systems for power steering and braking while future developments may feature a pump for each road wheel and a totally active system (the Activa is, in truth, reactive, albeit its reactions are so quick as to almost deserve the appellation) which reads the road surface ahead of the car and provides precisely the correct amount of suspension travel.

Above a schematic of the DS showing the suspension system.

Below a publicity shot for the DS showing the interaction between hydraulics, represented by water and air represented by the ballons.

Above a schematic of the DS showing the braking system.

Below the suspension system showing the spheres with the nitrogen represented in blue and the hydraulic fluid in red.

Above - load (P) is placed in car and it sinks.

Left - manual ride height control in Xantia.

Above - height corrector (3) admits hydraulic fluid which "lengthens" the strut and raises the vehicle to its normal ride height.

Another advantage of the variable ride height was the ability to dispense with a conventional jack. To jack the car up, all that was required was to place it in the highest suspension position, place a simple stand under the car and then select the lowest suspension position. The two wheels on the side of the car under which the stand is placed lift themselves off the ground.

According to recent reports, other car manufacturers, notably Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Benz licenced the system which was also used on Berliet trucks. Similar systems are also used on some military vehicles.

In a recent development, at the heart of the system are the so-called 'spheres' one per wheel and one main accumulator as well as a dedicated brake accumulator on some models. The purpose of the main accumulator is to even out fluctuations in pressure.

On later cars fitted with antisink or Activa suspension, there may be as many as nine spheres. Each sphere consists of a hollow metal ball, open to the bottom, with the top and bottom of the sphere being separated by a flexible desmopan rubber membrane. The top is filled with nitrogen at high pressure, up to 75 bar while the bottom connects to the car's hydraulic fluid circuit. The high pressure pump powered by the engine pressurizes the circuit and the accumulator sphere. This part of the circuit is at between 150 and 180 bars. It powers the front brakes first, prioritised via a security valve, and depending on type of vehicle, can power the steering, clutch, gearchange, etc.

It has been revealed that pressure goes from this circuit to the wheel spheres, pressurizing the bottom part of the spheres and rods connected to the wheel suspension. Suspension works by means of a rod pushing LHM into the sphere, compressing the nitrogen in the upper part of the sphere. Damping is provided by a two-way 'leaf valve' in the opening of the sphere. LHM has to squeeze back and forth through this valve which causes resistance and controls the suspension movements. This damper is far simpler and more reliable than those fitted to conventional vehicles and is also more efficient.

Height correction and levelling.

Car height correction works by height correctors connected to the front and rear anti-roll bars and permit more more fluid to travel under pressure to the spheres when it detects that the suspension is lower than the pre-determined ride height (e.g. the car is loaded). When the ride height is too high (e.g. after unloading) fluid is returned to the system reservoir via low-pressure return pipes. Height correctors act with some delay in order not to correct regular suspension movements. Rear brakes are powered from the rear suspension spheres. Because the pressure there is proportional to the load, so is the braking power. Furthermore, under heavy braking, hydraulic fluid is removed from the rear suspension causing the tail to drop providing inbuilt anti-dive.

In a recent development, spheres are not subject to mechanical wear, but do suffer pressure loss, mostly from nitrogen diffusing through the membrane. They typically last between 60,000 and 100,000 km. Spheres once had a threaded plug on top for recharging. Newer spheres do not have this plug, but it can be retrofitted. The symptom of pressure loss is a hard ride.

Hydropneumatics are inherently superior to steel springs for reasons that are often misunderstood. In addition to the superb comfort, they also have advantages related to car handling and control efficiency, solving a number of problems which are inherent in the use of steel springs.

Sources indicate that the hydropneumatic system is a progressive spring-rate suspension, in other words the more it is compressed, the stiffer it becomes. This results in a suspension which is extremely soft in its initial movement (far softer than a steel spring) but which becomes harder and harder as it is compressed (far stiffer than a steel spring). This is because of the inherent properties of a gas: halve its volume and its pressure doubles. When the suspension operates, the ram pushes oil into the sphere, thereby altering the volume (and therefore the pressure) of the gas. Usually steel-sprung cars are either too soft ("comfortable"), or too stiff ("sporty"), or some intermediate compromise, while hydropneumatics offer "two cars in one". Many manufacturers supply composite steel springs with a soft course and a stiff course - two different, discrete spring rates, whereas hydropneumatics offer an infinite number of rates.

According to recent reports, this also ensures that the suspension's spring-rate (hardness) is continuously adapted to the vehicle load. Thus when the car is unladen, the pressure within the spheres is in balance. If a passenger enters the car, this pressure becomes higher by the value of his or her weight (the gas in the spheres is compressed to an equal degree, i.e. has now become "harder") and the car will have lost some height, so the self-leveling system immediately reacts and brings the car up to the predetermined ride height. The result is that the spring rate is kept constant, regardless of the load of the car. In other words, a fully loaded car will be as equally well controlled as a car with just one passenger. With a steel-spring car, either the car would be set up to be comfortable with 1-2 passengers but getting too soft as more weight is added (becoming uncontrollable under full payload), or it would be too stiff with 1-2 passengers and okay on full payload. This effect is especially pronounced at the rear where the designer of a steel-sprung car has to make a compromise because the rear suspension has to be able to deal with a large range of loads. Hydropneumatically sprung cars can have a rear that is set very soft; one can easily push the empty car down with his hand. When a load is added, it stiffens as much as necessary. Steel-sprung cars need to have rear springs much stiffer than necessary for comfortable daily driving.

The self-levelling system ensures that there is always the same suspension travel available irrespective of load. Furthermore, the self-levelling function also rids suspension design of a number of unwanted compromises that designers of conventionally sprung cars have to make since the suspension is always functioning around one predetermined position, no matter the car's load, the various suspension-geometry complications become a much simpler equation to solve. A hydropneumatic suspension operates at ideal angles at all times and under all conditions. The ride comfort is excellent and never wallows uncontrollably in the way that an equally softly sprung car on steel springs would do.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles Unified, the second-largest US school district, has quietly disabled AI Overviews in Google search on student devices, AP reported.
  • Recent findings suggest that los Angeles Unified, the second-largest school district in the US, has switched off AI Overviews in Google search on student devices, the Associated Press reported.
  • It has been revealed that the district, which has about half a million students, made no formal announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles Unified, the second-largest US school district, has quietly disabled AI Overviews in Google search on student devices, AP reported. Google states schools that turn off AI entirely will lose search, and some districts are building workarounds or weighing other search engines.

Recent findings suggest that los Angeles Unified, the second-largest school district in the US, has switched off AI Overviews in Google search on student devices, the Associated Press reported. It is the largest district yet to work around Google’s refusal to offer schools search without AI.

It has been revealed that the district, which has about half a million students, made no formal announcement. Parents noticed the AI summaries had gone days after a school board meeting on November 13, said Bridie Lee of the parents’ group Schools Beyond Screens LA. The district has already stopped issuing Chromebooks to its youngest pupils.

LAUSD said it had “temporarily suspended” the feature to keep students’ experience “age-appropriate and safe.” It said it uses several layers of controls, including third-party filtering tools.

Earlier this month, Google said it would switch off Gemini and search for K-12 students by default, leaving schools to turn each one on. But it won’t offer search without its AI features. Schools that reject AI entirely will lose search, Google’s education chief Chris Phillips told The Fresh York Times.

That has drawn pushback even inside Google. More than 540 employees and contractors have signed a petition asking the company to let schools keep search without AI. In July, Common Sense Media called Google’s AI search an “unacceptable risk” for students.

Other districts are finding their own workarounds. Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia has built plug-ins that remove AI summaries, according to published reports. Some districts are looking at Bing and DuckDuckGo, which let consumers turn off AI answers.

“We have choices,” Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, told a school board committee. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.”.

Instead of an AI-free search, Google is testing a “guided learning” tool that walks students through problems step by step.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the newly introduced Dynamic Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, macOS 27.3 is launching next month alongside iOS 27.3 and more, and it includes a variety of newly introduced features for Mac customers. Here are three macOS 27.3 features coming soon.

It has been revealed that macOS already supports running Live Activities from your iPhone via iPhone Mirroring. But in macOS 27.3, Apple is adding native support for Live Activities from Mac apps.

The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the newly introduced Dynamic Island. But with macOS 27.3, the new feature expands to all Mac models and in a slightly different way.

Live Activities on Macs without a Dynamic Island will display in the menu bar. From there you can click to view full details, as seen above.

Safari introduces several upgrades across macOS 27.3, iOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3.

Industry observers note that vertical Tabs are one tentpole addition, providing a newly introduced option for how to view your tabs in Apple’s browser. When enabled, your tabs move from the top of the browser to the left side in a new column view.

Adaptive Dark Mode is another newly introduced feature. It automatically enables dark mode on many websites that don’t natively support it already. Finally, Siri AI gains support for new Safari actions, including the ability to interact with a full webpage using onscreen awareness, not just the parts that are currently visible.

In a recent development, do you use Markdown, the popular John Gruber-created plain text syntax? If so, macOS 27.3 has a welcome addition: support for rendering Markdown in Quick Look.

Rather than needing to open Markdown files in apps to preview formatted text, macOS now lets you just use Quick Look and see all of your Markdown syntax rendered properly with links, headings, bold, italics, and more.

You can learn more about Markdown here on John Gruber’s site, Daring Fireball.

Which macOS 27.3 additions are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me.
  • But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m at the moment using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….
  • The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m at the moment using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

Sources indicate that this device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

Industry observers note that what I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

It has been revealed that the size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

Industry observers note that when using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

In a recent development, my preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen.

In a recent development, while the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I mentioned when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

It’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an matter at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Sources indicate that split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI ).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

In a recent development, I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

In a recent development, the aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

In a recent development, I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the newly introduced Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

The Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Sources indicate that perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The glitch is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

In a recent development, the rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the concern, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

In a recent development, one of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller glitch than I expected it to be.

In a recent development, for example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

Recent findings suggest that I stated in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

My head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand newly introduced form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

In previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Representatives of NEURA Robotics, the Government of Aragón and Costa Group sign the memorandum of understanding.
  • German robotics firm NEURA Robotics has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government of Aragón and agri-food group Costa Group to open a NEURA Gym in Aragón by mid-2027.
  • In a recent development, german robotics tech giant NEURA Robotics plans to open a robot training centre in Aragón, Spain, by mid-2027, it noted on Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives of NEURA Robotics, the Government of Aragón and Costa Group sign the memorandum of understanding.

German robotics firm NEURA Robotics has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government of Aragón and agri-food group Costa Group to open a NEURA Gym in Aragón by mid-2027. The partners blueprint to invest in the double-digit millions of euros, with NEURA leading, and to add a zone for testing robots in real settings.

In a recent development, german robotics tech giant NEURA Robotics plans to open a robot training centre in Aragón, Spain, by mid-2027, it noted on Thursday. It has signed a memorandum of understanding with the regional government and Costa Group, an Aragonese meat and agri-food group.

In a recent development, the partners strategy to invest in the “double-digit millions of euros”, with NEURA taking the lead. They did not give an exact figure.

The site will be one of NEURA’s Gyms, where companies train robots on real tasks before putting them to work. Firms will bring their own processes, test them on different robots and check how well they perform.

Through NEURA’s Neuraverse platform, companies can keep the robot skills they develop private or license them to others for a fee.

“A organization that develops a valuable skill should benefit when others use it,” mentioned David Reger, NEURA’s founder and chief executive.

Costa Group will supply real problems from its farms and factories. The first projects will aim to cut physically demanding and repetitive work, before moving into logistics, cars and manufacturing. The University of Zaragoza will add research and train staff.

According to recent reports, the partners also initiative a “Physical AI Model Zone”, where robots can be tested in real working settings. Its scope and locations are still to be agreed, and any testing in public areas will need permits.

NEURA raised up to $1.4B in June, partly to expand its Gyms. It has since bought two companies. In Spain, Barcelona’s THEKER raised €73M in June for factory robots that learn on the job.

iPhone 18 was conspicuously absent from Apple’s annual September event this year. Instead, the tech giant launched iPhone 18 Pro and kept iPhone 17 around as the base model.

But the iPhone 18 is still coming, expected to launch in early 2027—likely February or March.

The basic design of the iPhone 18 is expected to stay unchanged as Apple prioritizes internal upgrades. Rumored upcoming features include a more powerful A20 chip with at least a slight RAM bump, plus increased battery life.

ProMotion is expected to be missing from the new model, which will still have a 60Hz display. And while massive rear camera upgrades are unlikely, a recent CAD leak suggests iPhone 18e might get a larger camera bump.

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone Air 2 will reportedly aim to address two of the top wishes owners had for the first-gen model. Those two upgrades are:.

By adding a second rear camera, iPhone Air 2 will at least offer camera parity with the base iPhone—something the original Air couldn’t with its single camera.

According to recent reports, battery life gains could ease concerns about the iPhone Air 2 running a full day on a charge. And hopefully the Air 2 will benefit from positive word-of-mouth about the first model.

Another tentpole addition is the A20 Pro chip, which might include one less GPU core than iPhone 18 Pro but otherwise be very similar.

Following the introduction of these three iPhone models in early 2027, Apple is expected to launch fresh Pro and Duo models in fall 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Verizon is in talks to buy Fidium, a fibre broadband operator owned by Searchlight Capital and BCI, for about $6B including debt, the Financial Times reported. A deal could come within weeks, as Verizon tries to win more home internet customers after buying Frontier.

Verizon is in talks to buy US fibre broadband operator Fidium for about $6B including debt, the Financial Times reported on Friday, according to Bloomberg.

Fidium is owned by Searchlight Capital Partners and British Columbia Investment Management Corporation (BCI). A deal could come in the coming weeks, the FT said, though another bidder may emerge and the talks may not lead to a takeover.

Verizon declined to comment. Fidium did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.

Industry observers note that the Illinois-based company sells fibre internet in more than 20 US states. It was called Consolidated Communications until last year, when it renamed itself after its fibre brand. Searchlight and BCI agreed to take it private in 2023 in a $3.1B deal including debt.

In a recent development, verizon has been buying fibre networks to catch up with rivals in home internet. Earlier this year, it closed its $9.6B purchase of Frontier Communications.

It has been revealed that growth has still been slow. Verizon added 314,000 broadband customers in the third quarter, below analysts’ estimates, even as it signed up twice as many new phone customers as expected.

It has been revealed that chief executive Dan Schulman told investors that customers increasingly prefer fibre to 5G-powered home internet. Since taking over last year, Schulman has cut retail jobs and argued that SpaceX would need up to $500B to match Verizon’s mobile network.

  • Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, my wife and I bought our first house. Along with all the other exciting things, it’s also let me spend a lot of time testing new smart home gear.

It has been revealed that one of the most notable and useful smart home accessories is a smart thermostat. Six months ago, I installed the Aqara Smart Thermostat W200, and it’s been a fantastic addition to our smart home setup … especially because it supports Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature. Here’s how it works.

Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward. I’d previously installed various Ecobee thermostats. The trickiest part this time was learning the intricacies of the fresh house itself, which the Aqara app did a good job of guiding me through.

I used the Aqara app for the installation and setup, like choosing an interface design for the thermostat’s display itself. But after that, I closed the app and haven’t opened it since. Everything now is managed through the Apple Home app, and I appreciate that the Aqara app lets me do this without any pushback. It doesn’t try to pull me back into it to sell me a subscription or show me ads.

This matters because the Aqara app is nothing to write home about. It has a lot of settings, but I don’t think it’s particularly elegant or user-friendly. You can choose from a small collection of different screensavers. The thermostat’s interface is similar to the app in that it’s very utilitarian, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing for quick manual temperature adjustments.

The Aqara W200 also has a mmWave radar sensor that detects your presence. When you walk up to it, that sensor detects your approach and the screensaver automatically goes away to reveal the controls. It’s also exposed to HomeKit and can trigger automations. Unfortunately, this isn’t particularly useful for me because of the thermostat’s awkward location.

The Aqara W200’s build quality is good enough. It’s primarily made of plastic, unlike higher-end smart thermostats that feature metal housing, so it doesn’t look super premium on your wall. It has a responsive 4-inch touchscreen. It has a small footprint overall, so you’ll likely need the included back trim plate if your previous thermostat required a larger opening in the wall.

The standout feature of the Aqara W200, though, is its support for Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature, which debuted as part of iOS 26. As of right now, the Aqara W200 is the only thermostat with Adaptive Temperature support available, though two more are coming next year as part of Apple’s new Home Collection suite.

It has been revealed that adaptive Temperature is Apple’s feature that will automatically adjust your thermostat’s temperature based on your preferences. It uses your location and the location of other home members to determine when to adjust the thermostat.

Once you enable Adaptive Temperature, you set your ideal temperature range for the following states:.

Recent findings suggest that my wife and I set our preferred temperature ranges for each scenario. I particularly appreciate the ability to set a different range for night, since we like it noticeably colder overnight than during the day.

After that setup process, Adaptive Temperature has worked in the background without any involvement from us. It passively uses all the information on our iPhones to make its decision.

“Your iPhone uses on-device intelligence to predict when you’re on your way home to bring it to the correct temperature by the time you get there, and adjusts the thermostat to save energy when you are far away from home,” Apple explains.

Adaptive Temperature uses your iPhone and other home members’ devices to determine when to adjust the temperature. “Home can learn daily routines to predict when you’re likely to arrive and adjust the temperature for you,” Apple notes. This includes things like your calendar events.

I can count on one hand the number of times we’ve had to manually adjust the thermostat since installing the W200, and most of those times were because we had guests with different preferences than ours.

Sources indicate that honestly, I thought I wrote this post months ago, but I guess it slipped my mind. I actually think there’s a pretty simple explanation for that, though. I installed the W200, enabled Adaptive Temperature in the Apple Home app, and haven’t thought about it since.

I think that’s a great endorsement of the Aqara W200 as a product. When I build a smart home, I want accessories that I can install, benefit from the “smarts” of, and never have to think about. That’s why I’ve also come to appreciate Lutron, which I’ve installed throughout my entire house. The Aqara W200 falls into that same bucket.

Between the Smart Thermostat W200 and UWB Smart Lock U400 (full review), Aqara powers two key pillars of my smart home, and I’ve been incredibly impressed with both.

Sources indicate that the Aqara Smart Thermostat W200 is also very reasonably priced. It retails for $159.99, but is at the moment on sale for $119.99.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI has filed counterclaims against Apple, accusing it of pressuring suppliers not to work on OpenAI’s devices and using broad employment agreements to stop engineers joining OpenAI, Bloomberg reported. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging theft of hardware trade secrets.

It has been revealed that openAI says Apple has pushed suppliers not to work on its devices, Bloomberg reported. It made the claims in a court filing in San Jose on Friday, hitting back at Apple’s trade-secrets lawsuit.

“Apple has responded to OpenAI’s anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI,” the company remarked in the filing.

According to OpenAI, Apple asks suppliers to name their OpenAI projects and the staff on them who once worked for Apple. It then tries to keep anyone who has worked on OpenAI products off Apple jobs. That makes suppliers wary of putting staff on OpenAI work.

Recent findings suggest that one supplier moved its OpenAI work to the night shift so it would not overlap with Apple work, which raised OpenAI’s costs, the filing says. Others have moved meetings with OpenAI so Apple would not see them.

OpenAI also takes aim at the contracts Apple staff sign. It states they treat almost everything workers learn as secret and stop them hiring away Apple staff for a year. It repeats its claim that a former worker who returned to Apple took more than 100 files about an unreleased OpenAI device.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg. It has mentioned before that it found no evidence for OpenAI’s claims.

According to recent reports, apple sued in July. It states OpenAI and its hardware chief Tang Tan used former Apple staff to get its secrets, and that OpenAI had a shared supplier copy an Apple metal-finishing method. In October, OpenAI agreed not to use the files Apple says were taken while the case goes on.

The fight hangs over OpenAI’s plans to sell devices designed with Jony Ive, starting with a doughnut-shaped speaker. The two once worked together to bring ChatGPT to Siri, a partnership that has since turned sour.

Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt.
  • High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago.
  • In a recent development, the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

In a recent development, the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone stated.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning.".

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Industry observers note that "We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she remarked.

Sources indicate that the lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, stated Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

According to recent reports, the overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he stated. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market.".

It has been revealed that in addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now.".

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she stated.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

According to recent reports, but there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

In a recent development, "We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin noted. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising.".

According to recent reports, it's also crucial to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, remarked R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

In a recent development, "That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder.".

  • The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit in a California court on Friday, striking back after the iPhone maker accused the AI lab of stealing top-secret information this summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI has countersued Apple, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets and threatening suppliers working on its upcoming devices. The filing escalates a legal fight that began with Apple’s lawsuit against OpenAI in July.

OpenAI has launched a new legal action against Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers, in an effort to “compete unfairly by any means available”.

The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit in a California court on Friday, striking back after the iPhone maker accused the AI lab of stealing top-secret information this summer.

According to recent reports, according to the report, OpenAI alleges Apple is “coercing and threatening” suppliers working with the ChatGPT maker. Its hardware ambitions include newly introduced personal devices following last year’s acquisition of Jony Ive’s “io” firm.

The complaint also claims Apple encouraged employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud accounts. OpenAI has previously characterized Apple’s case as an attempt to stop it from hiring Apple employees.

Apple’s original lawsuit names OpenAI, io Products, and former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan. Tan previously led iPhone and Apple Watch product design at Apple.

In a recent development, apple alleges confidential engineering information and hardware development details were taken to benefit OpenAI’s consumer device efforts. OpenAI has disputed those allegations.

The new action also follows OpenAI’s October claim that an employee who returned to Apple sent more than 100 confidential files about unreleased OpenAI hardware to personal accounts. Those files allegedly included device images, engineering data, and supplier information.

Apple responded at the time that its investigation had not located OpenAI confidential information. The firm remarked it requested more specific information to continue searching and would work with OpenAI to investigate the allegations.

Meanwhile, Apple has sought a preliminary injunction to prevent further use of its alleged trade secrets and won expanded access to evidence during discovery.

Apple’s original case is scheduled to go to trial on July 19, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we're closing in on the end of November, which means Thanksgiving is here and Black Friday deals are already in full swing. If there was ever a weekend to put your feet up after the big feast and lose yourself in something good from the top streaming services like Netflix, this is it.

We dug through the full list of everything coming to Netflix in November 2026 to pull out three gems worth your long weekend: a nightmarish anime set in a sunless world where people turn into plants to survive, a gripping true-crime docuseries on one of the most divisive murder trials in recent memory, and Netflix's first Nordic medical drama, shot inside a real former emergency room.

Whatever you're in the mood for this holiday weekend, these three highlights earn a spot on your watch list. Enjoy the family time (if you're celebrating right now) and buy yourself something shiny for Black Friday.

True crime obsessives, this one's ready and waiting for you. "The Trials of Karen Read" revisits one of the most divisive murder cases in recent memory: the death of Boston police officer John O'Keefe, found in the snow outside a Canton, Massachusetts home in January 2022. It also extends to the two trials that followed for his girlfriend, Karen Read, and her status as a potential suspect. The first ended in a mistrial in 2024, and the second, in 2025, ended in her acquittal.

Industry observers note that across three episodes, directors Danielle Johnson and Rob Miller follow the case from the initial investigation to the media spectacle it became, with the defense's claim that Read was framed in a police cover-up running underneath it all. It also includes interviews with jurors and with members of O'Keefe's own family. It's a twisty journey that's well worth investing in.

Watch "The Trials of Karen Read" on Netflix now.

If you're after an anime that's got a newly introduced and inventive (as well as disturbing) hook, here it is. "Fool Night" takes place a century into a sunless future, where thick cloud cover has choked out the light. Humanity survives by "transplanting" people into Spirit Flowers, plants that generate the oxygen everyone else breathes. A young man named Toshiro Kamiya chooses to undergo the procedure, and the result is just as bleak and strange as that sounds.

This series marks the first team-up between Sunrise (the "Gundam" studio) and Shaft (of "Puella Magi Madoka Magica"), directed by Atsushi Yukawa of "Space Dandy" and adapted from Kasumi Yasuda's manga. And it promises to be a great-looking journey that you won't forget.

Watch "Fool Night" on Netflix on Nov. 26.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that. They don’t tell it where in the room you are, though. That’s why these types of automations end up being all-or-nothing type things: you walk into a room, and every light comes on at full brightness, whether you came in to read at your desk or to grab something off the counter. The Meross MS605 splits its detection range into three distance zones, and each of them demonstrates up in Apple Home as its own presence sensor so you can build automations around them.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Sources indicate that you’ll set the zones in the Meross iPhone app during setup, choosing a distance for each. Once the Meross MS605 is in Apple Home (via Matter), all three appear as separate presence sensors, and you can build automations for each individually. If you only want two, disable the third in the Meross app, and it disappears from the Home app as well.

Industry observers note that A bathroom is the obvious use case here for early mornings. Set the far zone to turn a lamp on at 5% and the near zone to bring up an overhead light, etc.

In a recent development, the same idea works anywhere the room has more than one job. A hallway can light the path dim from the far zone, then go to 100% when you get close. An office can keep the overheads on while you’re anywhere in the room and turn on the desk lamp when you actually sit down as well. I find it incredibly useful for overall dimming, though.

It has been revealed that the Meross MS605 uses mmWave radar and PIR together, which is the current best practice for presence detection. Meross says the radar picks up micro-movement, so it knows you’re there when you’re sitting still, and the PIR filters out things that move but aren’t warm, like curtains and a robot vacuum. There’s also a radar-only setting if you want it as well.

Range is up to about 20 feet for motion and 13 feet for presence, with each zone configurable within those limits. There’s a built-in light sensor, too, so you can gate your lighting automations based on actual room brightness instead of guessing when you’ll want it with a sunset/sunrise trigger.

The Meross MS605 is IP67-rated and operates from -4 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, so a covered porch, a garage, or a basement is all fair game for placing the sensor.

Recent findings suggest that the initial setup runs via the Meross app over Bluetooth, and the app is required afterward. Zones, sensitivity, presence-and-absence timing, recalibration, and firmware updates all live in it. Day-to-day control and automation happen in Apple Home, but anything you want to tune requires going back.

One minor thing to know before you mount somewhere hard to reach: changing settings over Bluetooth requires pressing a physical button on top of the sensor, so keep that in mind when configuring your settings and initially placing it.

The Meross MS605 unlocks some unique use cases with its three zones. Three zones from one sensor is a upcoming automation tool, and the IP67 rating means you can put it in places other presence sensors can’t go. It’s powered by a CR123A battery, which is included in the box.

The Meross MS605 is available on Amazon.

* Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc).

Industry observers note that this attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.

According to recent reports, how the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is an ordinary web request, which a connect-src rule can block; steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside connect-src.

The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML.

It loads Insds.js or gtage.js from an Amazon S3 bucket.

It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on /checkout only.

GET /_cf/ice fetches the relay details, and POST /_cf/rel sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named northbridgeads[.]com host.

In a recent development, every exchange that returned relay details used turn.cloudflare.com. The malefactor's answers listed only Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and receives data.

The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a SHA-256 digest, then run with eval.

At Lascana's checkoutâ¡, the skimmer sent our test card details this way.

â¡ This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured.

It has been revealed that check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a newly introduced card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.

Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how promptly you report, so act fast. For more information, see âAdditional resourcesâ below.

That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with.

Industry observers note that we saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below.

This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.

It has been revealed that loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.

A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.

Speaking of torrenting, CyberGhost has torrenting-optimized servers in 88 countries and dedicated gaming servers in the US, UK, Germany, and France. Add to this its NoSpy servers in Romania, which CyberGhost runs itself rather than renting from a third party.

It doesn't have a whole host of extra features, but the basics are all there and work well. Every server is RAM-only, its strict no-logs policy has been independently audited twice by Deloitte, and its Romanian headquarters sits outside the Five, Nine, and Fourteen Eyes alliances.

Recent findings suggest that cyberGhost isn't without its drawbacks, though. It only supports seven devices, which is below the industry standard of 10. If you need to cover more devices, we reckon Surfshark ($2.49 per month for Surfshark One) or PIA ($1.49 per month) are better bets this Black Friday, as both offer unlimited simultaneous connections. CyberGhost's iOS app is also noticeably weaker than its desktop apps, with no kill switch or split tunneling.

According to recent reports, that noted, CyberGhost isn't promising to be an all-in-one VPN. If streaming is your main reason for getting one, CyberGhost is hard to beat at this price. Don't leave it too late, though – this $1.59-a-month deal ends soon, so grab it while you still can.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chile’s national competition authority, Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the tech giant of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases.
  • As reported by Reuters, Chile’s competition watchdog is seeking an $80 million fine against Apple, along with a court order requiring a series of changes to the organization’s App Store policies.
  • In its complaint, the FNE says (translation ours):.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chile’s national competition authority, Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the tech giant of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases. Here are the details.

As reported by Reuters, Chile’s competition watchdog is seeking an $80 million fine against Apple, along with a court order requiring a series of changes to the organization’s App Store policies.

In its complaint, the FNE says (translation ours):.

The defendant has violated Article 3, paragraphs one and two, subsection (b), of Decree Law 211 by abusing its dominant position through practices that prevent, restrict, or hinder free competition, or have the potential to do so, in the markets for app distribution and the distribution of paid digital goods within apps, both on the iOS operating system nationwide, from at least 2019 to the present day.

The FNE goes on to say that Apple forbids both sideloading and alternative app marketplaces, requires app developers to exclusively use the organization’s In-App Purchase system to sell digital goods and services within their apps, and restricts their ability to inform consumers about or direct them to alternative payment methods.

It then goes on to claim that “these anticompetitive practices have allowed the defendant to ensure that the App Store is the only channel for downloading apps,” adding that this “has led to a degradation of the consumer experience and allowed Apple to secure profits that it would not obtain without such practices.”.

Throughout the 50-page filing, the FNE draws on regulatory and judicial precedents from other jurisdictions, some involving ongoing disputes, to support its arguments that Apple’s restrictions are anticompetitive and that its privacy and security objectives can be achieved through less restrictive means.

That includes Apple’s agreement with Brazil’s competition authority, the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, the Epic Games v. Apple ruling in Australia, regulatory and judicial developments in Japan, and the lifting of anti-steering restrictions in the US.

At one point, the FNE even suggests that Apple knowingly maintained anticompetitive practices in the country, despite regulatory and judicial developments elsewhere:.

In a recent development, furthermore, there is evidence suggesting that the defendant was aware of the unlawfulness of its conduct, given the existence of precedents in other jurisdictions involving facts similar to those alleged in this complaint, which demonstrate the anticompetitive nature of the alleged practices. Nevertheless, Apple decided to maintain its restrictions in Chile, as well as in other jurisdictions where it has not been compelled to remove them or has not agreed with the relevant authority to eliminate or modify them.

After presenting its case, the FNE asks Chile’s antitrust court to:.

Additionally, the FNE asks the court to require Apple to implement these measures “in good faith, such that it may not impose any other technical or contractual restrictions, or commercial conditions, that undermine their purpose,” to cease the alleged anticompetitive practices, and to cover the legal costs of the proceedings.

It also leaves room for the court to impose any additional measures it deems appropriate, particularly those aimed at facilitating access to alternative channels for app distribution and the sale of digital goods.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and will enhancement this post if the company responds.

You can read the FNE’s full complaint here (in Spanish).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella revealed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft states its newly introduced AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella revealed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft states its newly introduced AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

Sources indicate that “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft mentioned. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also unveiled Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft mentioned, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s upcoming Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

It has been revealed that “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft noted.

The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. At the moment in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up rapidly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

Sources indicate that microsoft also declared that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft revealed a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft revealed last year, is the firm’s observability platform. Microsoft noted Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft revealed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft said. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

Sources indicate that “Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft mentioned. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise intends.
